activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: A 'best before' date marks when a food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe, so sealed food past that date may still be safe to eat.
story:
The food bank ran out of the library basement on Tuesday afternoons, which struck Simon as strange until he understood that the library was simply the one building in the neighbourhood everyone already entered without shame. He had signed up because his college applications wanted evidence of character, a phrase he distrusted, and because Ms. Kovalenko, who ran the program, had said they needed hands. She handed him a hairnet and a pair of gloves and put him at the sorting table beside Gavyn, whom he knew vaguely from chemistry.

The table held a cratesful of dented donations, and the work was simple: check the dates, sort the good from the bad. Simon picked up a can of chickpeas and saw the stamp, best before the third of last month. He set it in the discard bin without thinking, then hesitated over a second can, tomato paste, a week past its date. He threw that one out too.

Gavyn watched him do it. "You're getting rid of a lot."

"Past date," Simon said. "That's the rule, isn't it?"

"That's not what the date means." Gavyn held up a can of his own, turning it so the stamp caught the fluorescent light. "Best before is about quality, not safety. It marks when the food's quality may start to decline, not when it becomes unsafe. If it's sealed and stored right, it may still be safe to eat after that." He said it flatly, the way he said everything, and dropped the can into the keep crate.

Simon stood there with the tomato paste already buried under coffee tins. He had never actually considered what the date was for; he had predicated his whole understanding of food safety on it, the way you predicate a proof on a given, without asking whether the given was sound. "So everything I threw out," he said.

"Probably fine. Fish it out if you want."

He did want to, and he didn't. The discard bin was public in a way that embarrassed him; Dylan was two crates down, and Ms. Kovalenko moved along the shelves with a clipboard. Simon reached in anyway, past the coffee tins, and retrieved the tomato paste, the chickpeas, a box of crackers so far past its date that he held it up for Gavyn to judge.

"That one I'd toss," Gavyn said. "Sealed, technically, but a year is a lot of quality to lose."

So there was a line somewhere, and nobody had drawn it for him. Simon spent the next hour looking for it, can by can, and found that he could not always tell whether he was deciding or guessing. Dylan drifted over at one point, watched him deliberate over a jar of honey, and said, "It's honey, man. Honey outlives us all."

"That's not how it works," Simon said, and then, less certainly, "I don't think that's how it works."

Ms. Kovalenko stopped behind them on her clipboard round. She didn't say anything about the dates; she only noted how much they'd cleared and told Dylan the pasta shelf needed facing. But on her way past she put a laminated sheet on the table, the kind of thing the health department issued, and Simon read it while his hands went on sorting. The sheet said what Gavyn had said, in slightly more official language, and added nothing he could use to find the line.

He thought about his grandfather, who kept an ascetic fridge, bare shelves, everything accounted for, and threw out milk the day before its date as a matter of principle. Simon had always considered that a kind of discipline. Now it looked more like a pundit's certainty, an opinion held louder than the evidence warranted. But the opposite certainty was available too, the one that said nothing ever needed discarding, and he had watched a documentary where a cheerfully bearded man ate years-old canned goods and called it activism, and Simon hadn't trusted him either.

At the end of the shift Ms. Kovalenko asked him to log the totals. He counted the keep crate, then counted the discard bin, which held four items, each one he had chosen deliberately, and wrote both numbers in the columns. Four felt either careful or arbitrary, depending on what the dates actually meant, which he still did not fully know. Gavyn pulled off his hairnet and said, "Same time next week?"

"Yeah," Simon said, and turned back to the sheet, running his thumb along the laminated edge of the line about quality and decline.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A violin's four strings are tuned in perfect fifths to G, D, A and E, from lowest to highest.
story:
The auditorium smelled of dust and radiator paint, and Jaxon had the place to himself until four o'clock, which was the whole point. Ms. Berg had left the sign-out sheet on the piano bench, and he had written his name in the 3:10 slot with a determination that felt, even to him, slightly embarrassing. The violin lay in its battered case like a patient waiting for a diagnosis. He had been "learning" it for six weeks, which so far meant producing sounds that made the janitor wince through two closed doors.

He wanted one thing, and it was small enough to say out loud but he never had: at the spring showcase, he wanted to play the sixteen bars of his aunt's old reel without stopping, without his hands seizing up the way they did whenever Avery was in the room. Avery had played cello since he was eight and had a way of saying "you'll get there" that landed like a coin tossed to a beggar. Juliane, who was learning violin alongside him and was somehow already better, had a way of not saying anything at all, which was worse.

The trouble today was the same trouble as every day. He would set his fingers for a note, and the sound that came out would belong to some other string, and he would stand there in the empty rows of folded seats trying to cogitate his way backward through what his left hand had just done. Twice he put the bow down and stared at the instrument as if it were withholding information. The third time, he threw the bow onto the music stand, and it clattered off onto the stage with a petulant snap that he immediately regretted, because the sound carried and because throwing things was the kind of thing his father did.

"That's not how you treat the only violin that likes you," Juliane said from the wings. She came out carrying her own case and a sandwich, sat down on the edge of the stage, and started eating as though she had bought a ticket. "Sorry. I signed up for 3:40 but the door was unlocked."

"It doesn't like me. That's the problem." He picked up the bow and checked the stick for cracks. "I put my finger down for one note and another one comes out. Every time. I can't even tell which string I'm on."

Juliane swallowed and wiped her mouth with her wrist. "You don't know the order?"

"Of what?"

"Of the strings. God, Jaxon." She set the sandwich down, plucked his open string, then walked her fingers down the pegs. "Lowest to highest: G, D, A, E. My cousin told me a way to remember it. Good Dogs Always Eat. She made me say it fifty times until I stopped mixing up the D and the A."

"Good Dogs Always Eat," he repeated. It felt like a joke, and also like a rope thrown to someone in water. He looked down at the instrument and, for the first time, actually looked: four strings, thickest to thinnest, a ladder from G up to E, each one a fifth above the last, spaced evenly like the whole thing had been designed by someone sensible. "Wait. They're all the same distance apart?"

Juliane shrugged. "My cousin said fifths, whatever that means. I just know the words." She had gone back to her sandwich, entirely uninterested in what he was now doing, which was plucking each string in order, G, D, A, E, whispering the sentence under his breath, then closing his eyes and doing it again. On the third try he found the A string with his finger without looking, and the note rang out into the empty seats and came back a half second later, and something in his chest unlocked a single notch.

"Say it again," he said.

"Good Dogs Always Eat. It's not poetry."

"It's enough." He lifted the bow. The reel started badly, as it always did, but at the fourth bar his hand drifted toward the wrong string and he caught it, because he knew, actually knew, where he was. He finished the sixteen bars with two squeaks and a rhythm that stumbled on the turn, and when he lowered the bow Juliane was clapping with the two nearest fingers of one hand, deadpan as a court stenographer.

"You stopped," she said.

"I didn't stop. I slowed down. Those are different crimes with different levels of culpability."

Juliane laughed so hard she had to set the sandwich on the stage. "Play it again," she said. "I'll count you in."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The word diploma comes from a Greek word meaning "paper folded double," from the earlier practice of folding official documents.
story:
The party was in Colin's backyard, which his father had strung with lights that kept buzzing out, so the whole evening had a flickering, unreliable quality. Kevin arrived with his diploma folder under his arm because his mother had insisted he bring it, saying the relatives would want to see it, and then no relatives had asked. He set it on the table between the chip bowl and a cooler of soda, where it looked like a placemat.

He found Keira by the fence, holding a cup she wasn't drinking. They had applied to some of the same schools, and she had heard back from all of hers before he had heard back from any of his, which neither of them had mentioned since March. Colin had heard back from none of his, having applied to exactly one, a program in diesel mechanics that his irascible grandfather had declared a waste of a boy who could do calculus. Colin's position, stated often, was that his grandfather could be propitiated with a steady paycheck by Christmas.

"You didn't open yours," Keira said. "At the ceremony. Everyone else held theirs up like a fish they'd caught."

"Am I supposed to open it here?"

"It's a party. That's what the party is for."

Colin came over with the chip bowl, refilled without being asked, a habit his mother had trained into him like a reflex. He picked up the folder first, weighed it, and said, "For all you know it's blank inside. It could be a menu." This was exactly the kind of thing Kevin had been half afraid of since the ceremony, that the folder was a prop and the real document existed only in some office where a clerk had misspelled his middle name.

He opened it. The paper was flat, unfolded, printed once, sealed at the bottom with a sticker bearing the school's crest. Keira leaned in. Colin leaned in. Somewhere behind them the lights buzzed out and came back.

"It's not even folded," Colin said. "That's the whole thing? One sheet?"

Kevin looked at it, and something his father had said over dinner in April surfaced, his father who read etymology websites the way other men read box scores. "The word diploma," Kevin said, "comes from a Greek word meaning paper folded double. They used to fold official documents." He said it flatly, and Keira laughed, and Colin said, "So we got the folder instead of the fold," and Kevin said, "We got the folder instead of the fold," and for a second the three of them stood there grinning at a flat piece of paper on a table between chips and soda, which was, he supposed, what an education came to.

Keira picked up her cup and finally drank from it. "My mom has this maxim," she said. "The ceremony is for the parents, the diploma is for the bureaucrat, and the party is for whoever shows up." She looked at Kevin. "You haven't said where you're going. People keep asking me if you've said."

The lights buzzed out again and stayed out. In the dark, someone's phone turned on, and then several, and Colin's voice rose over the noise of the party saying his grandfather would say this was a sign. Kevin closed the folder. He had, in fact, decided two weeks ago and told no one, having constructed in his head a small theory that the deciding was the part that belonged to him and the telling was the part that belonged to everyone else, and he could see, holding the folder in the phone-lit dark, that this theory was mostly a way of putting off a conversation that would be awkward. He could also see the opposite argument, that withholding it from Keira specifically was its own kind of statement, one he hadn't decided to make and was making anyway.

He put the folder back between the chip bowl and the cooler, took Keira's empty cup, and went to get her a refill, because Colin had already gone to check the fuse box and someone had to keep the table stocked. At the cooler he found Keira's father, who had been standing there for some minutes, and who said, "So I hear you're not saying where you're going," and Kevin, popping the tab, said, "I hear it's a good school," and Keira's father said, "She told me this morning. She's happy for you. She's been telling people since Tuesday." Kevin stood there with two cups, one hers and one his, both sweating in the dark, and it occurred to him that the secret had never been his to keep, only his to be the last to stop keeping. He handed her the cup when he got back. She said, "To the fold," and tapped her cup against his.

activity: going on a first date
knowledge_domain: going on a first date
fact: In Arthur Aron's 1997 study, pairs of strangers took turns asking each other 36 questions that grew gradually more personal, and they ended up feeling closer than pairs making small talk.
story:
The park had a coffee cart but no coffee shop, which Brody hadn't planned for. He'd read somewhere, or half-read somewhere, that first dates went better indoors, at tables, where there were menus to point at when the conversation failed. Instead there was a bench under an arboreal cathedral of oaks, a woman named Eliane who had texted him a shrugging emoji that morning, and the sound of somebody's dog asserting itself near the fountain.

"You said the park," Eliane said, sitting down with her cup held in both hands, as if warming them despite the July heat. "I assumed you were being ironic."

"I was being cheap," Brody said. "The cart takes cash only and I have four dollars."

"That's honest at least." She wore a sunburn starting at her collar. He had noticed it on the walk from the parking lot and decided not to mention it, a decision that already felt like its own small achievement.

They had met in a summer stats class, three weeks of shared calculators and one conversation about the professor's habit of saying "obviously" before anything that was not obvious. Talking then had been easy in the way talking is easy when there is a common enemy. Now the common enemy was silence, and it was winning. He asked about her brothers; she asked about his job shelving books at the library; both answers were fine and neither went anywhere. She tore the rim of her cup into a small, methodical confetti.

"Okay," she said finally, and the word arrived with the gravity of a verdict. "We have nothing to say to each other in the normal way. So we should do it the abnormal way."

"There's an abnormal way?"

"There's a study. I read about it for a psych thing last semester. Arthur Aron, 1997. He had pairs of strangers take turns asking each other thirty-six questions, and the questions got gradually more personal as they went. The pairs who did that ended up feeling closer than pairs who just made small talk." She said it flatly, like reading a citation off a card, then balled up her confetti. "I don't remember all thirty-six. We can make them up."

Brody considered this. Part of him, the part that had spent the drive over rehearsing anecdotes about the library's ghost-themed display table, wanted to propitiate the silence with one of those anecdotes instead, to offer it something safe. But another part, quieter and more stubborn, said the anecdotes were the problem, that they were small talk wearing costumes. He looked at her sunburn and her destroyed cup and the dog, which had now won whatever dispute it had been prosecuting by the fountain.

"Fine," he said. "But I get to go first, and I'm starting harder than the study probably did. Question one: what's a thing you've changed your mind about in the last year, not gradually, like a switch flipping?"

She laughed, one surprised note. "That's cheating. You're supposed to start with 'what would constitute a perfect day for you.'"

"Then we're not doing the study. We're doing a different study, with a sample size of two, and no control group." He felt the shape of the thing as he said it: not the study itself, exactly, and not the ordinary dodge of banter either, but something in between that he was willing to defend. "Aron gets the credit for the format. The content's ours."

"Then my answer is church," she said, after a pause long enough that he almost took the question back. "I stopped going. Nobody dramatic happened. I just sat there one Sunday doing the phonetics of the hymns in my head instead of the words, like I was learning a foreign language I already spoke, and I realized I'd been doing that for about two years." She looked at him. "Your turn is supposed to come after I ask you one. That's the whole mechanism. Turns. But you should say something now anyway."

He didn't have a switch-flip answer, he told her honestly; his mind changed the way bread went stale, so gradually that he couldn't name a day. His mother had tried for years to get him to want a real job, something with a ladder in it, and lately he'd noticed he'd stopped arguing, though whether that was agreement or just tiredness he couldn't say. He said that, and then kept going, past the part where he would normally have stopped and made a joke, and told her about applying to transfer schools in the fall and lying to his father about which ones.

"That's two questions' worth," she said. "You owe me."

"Then ask me a hard one."

She turned on the bench to face him, and the confetti drifted off her lap and settled in the grass, and the dog, victorious, trotted past them without a glance. "Question two," she said. "How do you know when you're done being honest and you've started performing honesty?"

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In a presidential system, the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and cannot be removed simply because the legislature disagrees with them.
story:
Charlie had promised Ms. Berg she would be at the community centre by six, which meant she had forty minutes before the polls closed and no finished assignment. Ms. Berg, who taught comparative government at the college two towns over, had arranged for Charlie, Ajay, and Savanah to observe a real election as the backbone of their essays, and the essays were due at nine. Charlie's essay question sat folded in her jacket pocket: compare how a parliamentary system and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government. She had written two paragraphs in three days, and both of them were wrong, she suspected, in ways she could not yet name.

The gym smelled of floor wax and wet umbrellas. Voting machines hummed against the far wall, and a line of voters in raincoats stretched past the bake-sale table, which Savanah was supposed to be minding but had abandoned the moment she spotted Charlie. Savanah's want was simple and enormous: she wanted footage of her grandmother voting for the first time in this country, a clip for the documentary she had been assembling since September. Her grandmother was due any minute, and Savanah had her phone held sideways, ready, mesmirized by the doors the way a fisherman watches the surface of a lake.

"Tell me you brought your notes," Savanah said without lowering the phone.

"I brought the question." Charlie unfolded the paper and held it out. Ajay arrived behind them, shaking water off his sleeves, and read it upside down.

"That's easy," he said. "My uncle argues about this every Thanksgiving. In India we had an election and the party with the most seats picked the prime minister. No separate vote for him at all. And if Parliament stops supporting him, he's finished. He has to go." Ajay snapped his fingers, then looked around as though the snap had been too loud for a polling place.

"So the legislature can just fire him," Charlie said slowly, "even if the voters chose his party on purpose."

"They don't fire him exactly, they withdraw confidence, but yes, out he goes. My uncle calls it efficient. My aunt calls it chaos."

Charlie stared at the line of voters, each one feeding a ballot into a machine, and something assembled itself in her head, the way two photographs overlaid on a light table suddenly show one image. Here it was the reverse. The president appeared nowhere on the local ballot at all, because the president had been elected separately, on a different day, for a fixed term. And that term, she understood now, was the whole point. A legislature that disagreed with the president, even a majority that disagreed, could not simply remove him for that reason alone. The disagreement would just have to continue, scheduled and stable, until the fixed term ran out. She turned to Ajay. "So in a parliamentary system the head of government survives only as long as the legislature supports him, and in a presidential system the president is elected separately from the legislature for a fixed term and can't be removed just because the legislature disagrees with them. Two completely different logics of power."

"Finally," Ajay said. "My uncle would like you."

"Which one is better?" Savanah asked. Her grandmother had come through the doors, removing a scarf, small and certain, and Savanah's attention drifted sideways with the camera.

Charlie tried to answer and found she could not do it cleanly. The parliamentary way made the government quick and answerable, but a single bad afternoon in the legislature could collapse it. The presidential way made the leader stubbornly stable, which sounded like a virtue until you imagined a president the legislature despised and the voters regretted, still seated, immovable, running out a term like a sentence. Each system protected something the other exposed. She said some of this aloud, and Ajay nodded along, and then Ms. Berg was beside them, checking her watch.

"Nine minutes," Ms. Berg said. "Grandmother first, documentary after, essays by nine. And Charlie, whichever system you argue for, I'd better see the other one given a fair hearing, or the whole thing is just a slogan." She moved off to steady a folding sign that a draught had tipped.

Savanah walked her grandmother to the machine, narrating softly for the microphone, and the old woman fed her ballot in with two hands, like planting something. Charlie sat on the bleachers with her notebook, writing fast, one stratum of argument laid over another, the bellicose uncle in her head insisting on stability while a quieter voice insisted on accountability, neither of them winning. The clock over the doors showed 6:53. She underlined her thesis, crossed it out, and wrote, "It depends on what you are most afraid of," which was either the strongest sentence she had ever produced or the weakest, and she would not know which until the grade came back.

The doors were being propped open for the last voters, and rain hissed in the parking lot. Savanah lowered her camera at last, and her grandmother, passing on her way out, touched Charlie's notebook with one finger and said, "Write it down before you forget it. Elections and girls our age, we change our minds fast."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: At a Passover Seder the youngest child present customarily asks the Four Questions from the Haggadah, beginning with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?'
story:
The kitchen at Aunt Ruth's house smelled of roasted chicken and something scorched at the bottom of a pot, which Uncle Danny was trying to disguise with extra gravy. Logan stood at the counter slicing brisket while his mother set out the good plates, the ones with the hairline crack she still refused to retire. Through the doorway he could see his little cousin Rosie, age six, sitting on the stairs with a paperback Haggadah open on her knees, mouthing words.

"She's terrified," said Madeline, dropping onto the counter stool beside him. She was his cousin too, eighteen, home from her first year of college, and she had appointed herself Rosie's coach. "She has to ask the Four Questions tonight. You know, the youngest kid at the Seder always asks them. Starts with 'Why is this night different from all other nights?' and she keeps freezing at 'different.'"

"Why doesn't she just read it off the page?"

"It's not a reading, it's a performance. Everyone stares at you." Madeline slid off the stool. "Come on, I need a second pair of hands."

Logan carried the brisket platter to the dining room, then found himself sitting cross-legged on the bottom stair while Madeline knelt in front of Rosie. The stairwell was dim, the wallpaper flocked and old, and someone had left the hall closet open so that coats spilled their cold outside air onto their ankles.

"Again," Madeline said gently. "Just the first line. Don't rush it. Enunciate, so Grandpa can hear you from the far end of the table, because he will not turn up his hearing aid, we've tested this."

"Why is this night," Rosie said, very small, "different from all other nights?"

"Perfect. Now the second question."

Rosie stared at the page. Her finger trembled under a line of Hebrew. Logan watched her lip start to wobble, and he remembered being eight himself, sweating through the same questions in this same stairwell while his grandmother prompted him in a whisper. He had not thought about that in years.

"Hey," Logan said. "Want to know a trick? When I did it, I was so nervous I looked at the ceiling and pretended I was asking the questions to the light fixture. Nobody could tell I wasn't looking at them, and the light fixture never judges."

Rosie looked up. "The light fixture?"

"It's a very sympathetic light fixture."

She tried the line again, chin lifted, voice steadier. Madeline caught Logan's eye over her head and mouthed thank you.

By the time they were called to the table, the candles were lit and the room had that hushed, formal warmth it only got twice a year. Grandpa presided over the Seder plate, pointing out the shank bone and the bitter herb with the gravity of a museum docent. When they reached the right page, he looked down the table, and Rosie sat up straight, gripped the Haggadah with both hands, and delivered the first question in a clear voice that reached even the hearing aid, which was, for once, on.

"Why is this night different from all other nights?"

Afterward, while the adults argued cheerfully about whether the second cup of wine counted before dinner, Logan carried empty glasses to the kitchen and found his mother drying the cracked plate. He had been turning something over all evening, the way you turn a stone in your pocket. At school his ethics teacher, Mr. Cho, kept pushing this idea that you had to either believe a tradition or dissect it, as if those were the only two positions available. But tonight Logan had watched Madelle coach a frightened six-year-old not because the questions were literally true or false but because the asking mattered, because a small girl standing up in front of fourteen relatives and getting through it was its own kind of proof of something. And at the same time he had read the English translations on the page and not believed a word of them, not really, and he did not think the two facts about himself canceled out. What he hadn't worked out yet was what to call the thing in between, or whether his grandfather, who clearly believed every word, would be hurt to know it.

He put the glasses down next to the sink. His mother handed him the towel.

"You did a nice thing with the stairwell coaching," she said. "Madeline told me. Rosie's been scared for a week."

"Madeline did the actual work. I just supplied a light fixture."

His mother laughed and put the cracked plate back in the cabinet, careful as always. From the dining room came the sound of Rosie, still riding her triumph, asking Grandpa if she could do the Four Questions again next year even if her baby brother was the youngest by then. Grandpa said they'd negotiate. Logan dried the last glass and went back in to see how the negotiation would go.

activity: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
knowledge_domain: to solve projectile motion problems by separating horizontal and vertical velocity components
fact: Ignoring air resistance, launch angles that add up to 90 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same range on level ground at the same speed.
story:
The playground at the edge of the school grounds had one piece of equipment nobody used anymore, a wooden fort with a sagging tower, and Annabelle had claimed it as her study post since September. She sat on the tower's platform with her physics textbook open across her knees, the pages fluttering when the wind came through the chain-link fence. Below her, Kieran was setting up the projectile launcher they had signed out from the lab, bolting it to a picnic table with a clamp he had borrowed from the shop teacher without asking.

"You have it at thirty degrees," Annabelle called down, shading her eyes. She had spent the whole week trying to separate the horizontal and vertical components of velocity in her head, and the numbers kept sliding together like wet paint. Ms. Foster had marked her last test with a single red bracket around the entire second page and the word "components" underlined twice, which Annabelle had taken first as an insult and then, after two nights of rereading, as a kind of map.

"Thirty is boring," Kieran said. "Everything goes flat and dies." He cranked the launcher up until the protractor taped to its hinge read sixty, loaded a yellow plastic ball, and fired. The ball climbed steeply, hung for a moment at the top of its arc, and came down in the woodchips near the fence. Annabelle marked the spot with a red flag from her bag of supplies.

Then, out of a stubbornness she could not quite explain even to herself, she climbed down, reset the angle to thirty, and fired again. The ball skimmed out low and fast, and Annabelle watched it, trying to see what she had only ever drawn: the same launch split into two independent motions, one gliding sideways at a steady rate, one falling and rising as if it had been dropped straight down. The ball landed beside the red flag, close enough that she knelt and pushed the flag into the ground exactly between them.

"Hey," Kieran said, coming over. "That's the same spot."

"No. I moved the angle." She showed him the protractor. Thirty. He looked at the flag, at the faint twin dents in the woodchips, back at the launcher.

"You messed something up," he said, and fired at sixty again himself, standing back with his arms crossed like a man awaiting an apology. The ball rose, hung, fell. It landed a hand's width from the flag. Neither of them said anything for a while. A toddler at the far end of the playground shrieked and was scooped up by a parent, and the swings creaked on their chains in the wind.

Annabelle sat down on the edge of the picnic table and worked through it the way she now understood she was supposed to, the way she had failed to on the test. The two components were not a taxonomy of separate problems to be memorized, she thought, but a way of prediсating the whole motion on two simpler ones, each minding its own business. At thirty degrees the ball spent little time in the air but hurried sideways; at sixty it lingered twice as long but ambled. Somewhere in her notebook the algebra was already waiting, though she could not yet make the symbols do what the woodchips had just done. What she could not decide was whether the fact she had stumbled onto, that these two angles, thirty and sixty, summing to ninety degrees, gave the same range at the same speed, was a coincidence of the numbers or something she should have been able to predict. She was honest enough to admit she did not know yet, and honest enough to find that bearable, which was new.

Ms. Foster came along the fence path with her coffee, the way she did on Thursday afternoons, and stopped at the table. She looked at the flag, the protractor, the two dents. "Complementary angles," she said mildly, tapping the protractor. "They call them that." Then she sipped her coffee and kept walking, and Annabelle stared after her, half delighted and half certain she had just been teased, because Ms. Foster had said nothing else at all.

"It's like she knew we'd be here," Kieran said.

"She signed out the launcher to us." Annabelle turned the yellow ball over in her hand, feeling the scuff mark where it had struck the ground twice in the same place, and wondered whether her whole course, maybe her whole autumn, had been quietly arranged toward this table. She set the ball in the launcher, eased the hinge to forty-five, and pulled the trigger.

activity: to implement a binary search and explain why it beats a linear search on sorted data

fact: Programmers describe linear search as O(n), meaning its work grows in step with the list, and binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size.
story:
The robot had missed the block for the third time in the practice round, its arm sweeping past the mark by a full second, and Mathis knelt on the gym floor with the laptop balanced on one knee and watched the log scroll. Somewhere in a sorted array of eight hundred calibration values, the code was hunting for the one that matched the sensor reading, and it was doing it the way he had first written it, by starting at the top and checking each entry in turn. He had scribbled something on the whiteboard an hour ago, a note to himself, and now Ashlee was standing in front of it with her arms crossed.

"What is O log n," she said. "Is that a typo?"

Mr. Taylor, who had been circulating between the six tables in the auxiliary gym, stopped beside her and tapped the marker trough. He didn't say anything. He had this way of waiting, as if whatever he already knew would calcify into something useless the moment he handed it over, so he held it back and let the room stay turbid with half-formed ideas a little longer.

"Sort of a typo," Mathis said, still watching the log. "It's supposed to be O(log n). Big O, then log n." He stood up and crossed to the board, and it occurred to him, with a small strange thrill, that he had written down a thing he could not yet defend.

Liliana spun a chair around and sat on it backward. "Explain like we're the robot," she said. "The robot is dumb."

"Okay, so." He picked up the marker, then put it down, because drawing would make it look more certain than it was. "The values in the array are sorted. We sorted them when we calibrated. And I kept ignoring that, like it didn't matter, but it's the whole point. If you're looking for a word in the dictionary, you don't start at Aardvark."

Ashlee narrowed her eyes. "You open it in the middle."

"You open it in the middle, you see you're too far, you throw away half the dictionary in one move. Then you do it again. Eight hundred values, and each guess cuts what's left in half, so it's a handful of guesses instead of eight hundred." He heard himself say it and thought, is that actually right, or is that a story I'm telling myself about how it works? He counted on his fingers, halving eight hundred, and the number came out smaller than the fingers he had.

"But what we have now works," Liliana said, in the voice of someone who wanted very much for nothing to change before the elimination round at two o'clock. "It's slow, but it finds it."

"It finds it after the block is already past us." He pointed at the robot, sitting inert on the taped square, its arm still cocked at the angle of the miss. "That one-second lag, that's this. The search is eating our whole window."

Mr. Taylor cleared his throat. "Group votes on code changes in competition," he said. "House rule. Before anyone votes, Mathis, tell them what's on the board."

Mathis looked at the scribble again, at the little O with the log n after it, and understood that he was about to say something out loud that he had only half believed an hour ago. "Programmers describe linear search as O(n)," he said, "meaning its work grows in step with the list, and binary search as O(log n), meaning its work grows with the logarithm of the list's size." He said it slowly, and it felt less like reciting and more like testing whether the sentence held weight. "O(n) is the check-every-entry way. O(log n) is the cut-it-in-half way. That's the notation, that's what the scribble means."

There was a pause, the specific pause of a room deciding whether a person knew what they were talking about. He couldn't tell, from their faces, whether it had landed. Maybe that was the honest thing about it, he thought; he had brought together two things, the way he liked to hunt through problems and the way the dictionary had always worked, and the notation was just the grown-up name for the second one, the way every species of this particular trick belonged to the same genus of thinking. Whether he could implement it in ninety minutes was a separate question entirely, and he let it sit there, unanswered, rather than pretend.

"All right," Liliana said. "Move for a vote."

Ashlee raised her hand halfway, then all the way. "Second," she said, and pulled the laptop toward herself to start the timer.

activity: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
knowledge_domain: the idea that news outlets are owned by companies or people whose interests can shape coverage
fact: Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky's 1988 book Manufacturing Consent argued that news is shaped by five 'filters', the first of which is the ownership of media by large corporations.
story:
Kate came to the library on a Thursday with a real problem: the school board had voted to cut the library's hours, and the student paper, which she edited, was going to print its last issue of the year in nine days. She had one article, half of a second, and a hollow feeling where the editorial should have been.

She found Ruben at the back table with his shoes hooked on the rung of his chair, reading a battered paperback with a cracked spine. She could smell the old glue of it from across the room, that sweet dusty smell the library kept in its corners like a resident. Manufacturing Consent, the cover said, in type small enough to apologize for itself.

"You're reading that for Ms. Yilmaz's class?" Kate asked, dropping her bag.

"Extra credit, originally." He turned the book toward her. "Now it's ruining my life. Every time I open a news app I sit there wondering who owns it." He tapped a page. "It's by Edward Herman and Noam Chomsky, 1988. They argued news gets shaped by five filters. Guess what the first one is."

"Editors?"

"Ownership. Big corporations owning the media." He said it lightly, the way you'd report the weather, but Kate sat down anyway.

She remembered, suddenly, a Saturday two winters ago, when her father had stood in the kitchen prognosticating about the local paper, declaring with total confidence that it would fold within a year because its corporate owner had bought it only to strip it. She had been fourteen and had thought he was being paranoid. Now she tried to remember whether it had folded. She thought it had.

"What are the other four?" she asked.

"Money, sourcing, flak, ideology, roughly. But ownership comes first, and it's the one I keep noticing." Ruben pulled up his phone and showed her the ownership chain behind the outlet that had covered the school board vote. The chain led to a company that also sold the district its software. Kate leaned closer. The screen was warm from his pocket and smelled faintly of pencil shavings, which made no sense, and she noticed it anyway.

The vote coverage itself was strange now that she reread it. The article had quoted the superintendent twice, a board member twice, and a parent once. It had not mentioned that the library hours were being cut in the same semester the district signed a new contract for the software, or that the paper's own district-run website ran on it. "We're not exactly an archipelago of independent islands," Ruben said, waving a hand at the shelves around them. "More like one island with a lot of boats tied to the same dock."

Kate opened her notebook. Her want was simple and she said it out loud: "I want to write that the library cuts are connected to the software contract, and I want people who read the paper to know why the daily didn't touch it."

"Then you have to be careful," Ruben said. "The book doesn't prove every story is a lie. It's a filter, not a conspiracy. You still have to check the contract yourself."

So they did. Ms. Yilmaz, who kept the library's records, printed the board minutes from the public terminal, and Kate sat on the floor between the stacks with the pages fanned across her knees, the carpet releasing its smell of vacuumed dust. The contract was real. The figures were real. But when she looked for the connection to the cuts, the minutes only showed them voted the same night, by the same majority. Causation was not there on the page, and she could not conjure it.

The library closed at five now, earlier than it had before the vote, and the guard began his slow circuit at four forty. Kate gathered the minutes while Ruben held the door. Outside, the cold found the gap at her collar. She still had nine days, one solid fact, one honest gap between what she suspected and what she could prove, and a first sentence already forming, something like: The library closes early now, and here is who owns the silence.

"We could ask Yosef to design a chart of the ownership chain," Ruben said. "He owes me from the chess tournament."

Kate zipped her bag over the photocopied minutes. "Tell him to leave room for the parts we don't know."

activity: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
knowledge_domain: to critique a painting by Frida Kahlo using formal analysis of colour, composition and symbolism
fact: The Surrealist André Breton described Kahlo's art as "a ribbon around a bomb," though Kahlo herself later rejected the Surrealist label.
story:
The print Ms. Gupta had taped to the whiteboard was Kahlo's self-portrait with a thorn necklace, and Carson had been staring at it for six minutes without writing anything. Around him the art room smelled of turpentine and the burnt coffee the teacher kept on the back counter. His worksheet had three columns, one each for colour, composition, symbolism, and each was empty except for the heading he had copied from the board in careful print. The problem was that he did not know how to look at a painting the way Ms. Gupta wanted. He knew how to look at a basketball defense, how to find the seam in a zone, but a picture just sat there.

Talan leaned over from the next table. "You could just say it's Surrealist and be done," he said. "My sister did that last year and got a B."

"It's not Surrealist," Leo said, without looking up from his own paper. "I read that Breton called it that, he said her work was like a ribbon around a bomb, but Kahlo didn't want the label. She rejected it later." Leo said it flatly, the way he recited stats, and went back to his notes.

Talan rolled his eyes. "So she painted melting clocks and whatever and just didn't like the name?"

"She never said she didn't paint like that. She said the word didn't fit." Leo drew a small arrow in his margin. "There's a difference."

Carson wrote the phrase down, ribbon around a bomb, and underlined it twice. He looked back at the portrait. The leaves behind her were a green so saturated it seemed to vibrate against her brown skin, and the blood from the thorns ran in two thin lines toward the hummingbird, black and dead, hanging at her throat. He had missed the bird entirely the first three times he looked. Now he could not stop seeing it.

He tried both ways, the way Talan suggested and the way Leo implied. If he called her a Surrealist, the painting became a dream, a strangeness that came from somewhere outside Kahlo, from a movement Breton had assembled. But when he tracked the composition instead, the central axis of her body, the monkey's hand at her shoulder, the dark ribbon of the background foliage, the strangeness did not feel invented. It felt reported, like something she had actually worn. The colours did not float free of the world; they transmuted it, turning real blood and real leaves into something formal and exact. He wrote that down, then crossed out "exact" and wrote "precise," then crossed that out too and put "exact" back.

By the window, Ms. Gupta was watering the sad ivy on the sill, and the afternoon light moved across the print so that a strip of the foreground, where a sliver of littoral shoreline showed at the bottom edge of the portrait, glowed faintly blue. Carson noticed that Kahlo had put a slice of sea into a jungle. He could not decide whether that counted as symbolism or just as a fact of where she stood when she imagined herself.

His critique, when he finally wrote it, was an amalgam of the two positions, and he was honest enough to say so in the last line. He argued that Breton's phrase and Kahlo's rejection of it could both be true at once: the paintings could be a ribbon around a bomb and still belong to her alone, not to the movement. What he could not resolve, and said he could not, was whether calling the work Surrealist told you anything about the painting or only about the man doing the calling.

When Ms. Gupta collected the sheets, she read his last paragraph standing beside his desk, her finger moving under the words. "You're arguing with Breton and with Talan at the same time," she said.

"He started it," Talan said from across the room.

She set the paper down on Carson's desk, unmarked. "Bring me two more Kahlo paintings by Thursday and lose the word 'probably' from your conclusion."

Carson looked at the hummingbird, still hanging there, still dead, still bright green against her collarbone.

activity: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
knowledge_domain: to compute the integral of a function to find the area under a curve
fact: A Riemann sum approximates the area under a curve by adding up the areas of thin rectangles, and the integral is the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin.
story:
The math club met on Thursdays in the classroom by the creek, and on the first Thursday of March Mr. Weber announced that the regional competition was in nine days, which meant nine days to learn something Grayson had been avoiding all year. "Integrals," Mr. Weber said, writing the long S on the board. "You'll need the area under a curve. That's all I'm telling you." He set a stack of practice packets on the front desk and went back to his grading, because the rules of the club were that nobody taught anybody directly; you found things out or you didn't.

Sydnee pulled her chair up beside Grayson's and flipped to the last page, where a function curved down from the top left of the graph like a slide. "Find the area between the curve and the x-axis, from zero to four," she read. Grayson stared at the smooth swoop of it. There was no formula he knew for the area of a shape like that, no base times height, nothing in geometry that bent.

Jiya, two desks over, kept glancing at her watch, because she had a shift at four and had promised herself she would leave by three thirty. "Just count the grid squares," she said. Grayson did, ticking off the little boxes with his pencil, and got something close to fourteen. "That's not an answer," Sydnee said. "That's a guess wearing an answer's clothes." He had to agree. The squares were too coarse; half of them were cut through by the curve, and he'd been rounding up or down by mood.

That night, at the kitchen table, he cogitated on it longer than was probably healthy, turning the graph sideways, shading regions with the side of his pencil, until his mother asked whether he was drawing or doing homework and he couldn't honestly say. What finally occurred to him was so simple he distrusted it: the curve was only difficult because it was smooth, and smooth was just the limit of things that weren't. If he covered the region with rectangles, thin ones, standing side by side like fence pickets, each one had a plain ordinary area. Width times height. The heights came from the function itself; the widths he could choose.

He built a spreadsheet. Four rectangles gave him a total that was wrong in a way he could see, the rectangles' tops jutting above the curve or falling short of it. Eight rectangles got closer. Sixteen closer still. He sat there in the blue light of the screen adding more, dividing the span thinner and thinner, and watched the total settle, the way disturbed water settles, toward a number just under fourteen. He typed another column, halving the width again, and the change was so small it barely registered in the fourth decimal place. Whatever the true area was, the rectangles were crowding in on it.

At the next meeting he brought his laptop, and Sydnee leaned in to see the columns of shrinking widths. "What do you even call this," she said, and Jiya, who had stayed past her self-imposed deadline and kept checking the clock with a resignation that surprised her, said, "Riemann sum," before Grayson could. She'd found the name in the back of the packet, in a footnote whose provenance was unclear, maybe an old competition, maybe something Mr. Weber had pasted in from a textbook. "You add up the areas of the thin rectangles," she said, tapping the screen, "and the integral is the limit as the rectangles become infinitely thin." Grayson looked at his spreadsheet, at the widths marching toward zero, and felt the two halves of the thing fit together: the clumsy counting he'd done and the tidy symbol on the board were the same idea, one grown out of the other.

Then he discovered he'd been getting it wrong, or half wrong. When he placed his rectangle heights at the left edge of each slice, his totals came in low, because the curve was falling; when he placed them at the right edge, they came in high. For two evenings this bothered him more than he admitted to anyone, the sense that the answer depended on an arbitrary choice. On the third evening he added both columns to the spreadsheet and watched the gap between them shrink as the slices thinned, the low answer rising and the high answer falling until they agreed to more decimal places than the competition would ever ask for. The choice mattered less and less the thinner the rectangles became. He was honest enough with himself to notice what stayed uncertain: he had not proven anything, had only watched a screen, and for a moment on the walk to school he wondered whether watching could count as knowing.

On the Thursday before the competition, Sydnee tried the method herself on a rising curve and announced that she'd been wrong about the grid squares, that this was better, that she actually wanted to do it. Mr. Weber collected the packets without comment, though at the door he paused by Grayson's desk long enough to say, "Thursday. Bus leaves at seven," which was as close to encouragement as the club's rules permitted. Outside the classroom window the creek ran high with meltwater, the willows along its banks bent and bright, and Sydnee was already at the board, marker uncapped, drawing rectangles under a curve of her own. "Okay," she said. "Make it thinner."

activity: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
knowledge_domain: to direct a one-act play by blocking the actors' movements and running rehearsals
fact: Stage left and stage right are named from the actor's point of view while facing the audience, so they are the reverse of the audience's left and right.
story:
Claire had taped a rectangle of the gym floor with blue painter's tape and written ACT ONE on a clipboard that she had requisitioned, after some argument, from Ms. Somsak's supply cabinet. The one-act had to be performance-ready in nine days, which meant that tonight, the third rehearsal, was the night the actors had to stop holding their scripts and start moving. Kaylee stood downstage, gripping her script like a lifeline, and Willy leaned against the folded bleachers with the particular slouch of someone who had auditioned as a joke and then, to his own surprise, been cast.

"Okay," Claire said. "Kaylee, after your line about the letter, cross to the window. So you move stage left."

Kaylee walked to her right, toward the water fountain, script trailing behind her.

"No, the other left."

"I did go left," Kaylee said. "My left."

"That's not stage left," Claire said, and then stopped, because she realized she wasn't sure it wasn't. She had read the term in the blocking workbook and used it all evening as though it meant nothing, the way people say latitude when they mean weather. She looked out past Kaylee at the empty bleachers, the rows of folded seats where the audience would sit on the ninth day, and she turned her own body around to face the stage the way an actor faces an audience. When she did that, her left hand pointed at the water fountain, the side Kaylee had walked to, and something rearranged itself in her head like furniture being slid across a floor.

"Stage right," she said slowly. "You went stage right."

"You told me left," Kaylee said, not unkindly, but with the flat patience of someone who had stayed after practice on a Thursday.

"I did." Claire turned back around to face the bleachers, then faced away again, checking it twice the way you check a lock. "Stage left and stage right are from the actor's point of view, facing the audience. So they're the reverse of what the audience sees. Your left is their right." Saying it out loud felt like admitting she had been driving without a license, but Kaylee's face changed, and Willy pushed off the bleachers and walked to the fountain side, then pointed at it. "So this is stage right even though it looks like the left side of the stage to me."

"To us," Claire said. "To everybody watching."

They drilled it. Claire stood on the taped floor with her back to the bleachers and called directions, and the two of them crossed and recrossed until the words stopped requiring translation, until "stage left" moved Kaylee's feet before it moved her thoughts. Willy caught on faster than he let on. He had the disaffected air of a boy wasting his afternoon, but he hit his marks exactly, and once, when Kaylee flubbed a line, he prompted her so quietly that only Claire heard it. Kaylee's elocution, which had been mushy on the first night, sharpened as she moved; the walking seemed to carry the words, or the words carried the walking, and Claire wrote in the margin of her clipboard, blocking is not separate from the lines, and then crossed it out because it sounded like something a workbook would print.

By eight o'clock the gym had gone cold and the overhead lights buzzed with that metallic gym sound, and Ms. Somsak came through the double doors with her keys jangling. She watched the last ten minutes from the doorway, arms folded, saying nothing, which Claire had learned to read as approval. The scene ran clean. Kaylee crossed stage left on the letter line, Willy entered upstage right, and the moment they had walked toward each other and stopped a foot apart, close enough that Kaylee's next line came out different, smaller and truer, Claire felt the shape of the whole one-act assemble itself in the air above the tape.

"Good," Ms. Somsak said. "Very good. One thing. You've blocked it facing the main bleachers?"

Claire nodded, glowing.

"We can't use the main bleachers, the volleyball banquet is that night. The audience will be on the far side, folding chairs, facing the other way." Ms. Somsak jingled her keys and smiled at them all with terrible kindness. "So your stage left and stage right will be exactly backwards from everything you drilled tonight."

Claire stood very still on the taped rectangle, facing the empty folding-chair side of the gym, and raised her clipboard. "From the top," she said. "Kaylee, cross stage right."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The US average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year.
story:
The restaurant had pushed four tables together and taped a paper banner across the back wall that said CONGRATS CLASS OF 2023 in marker, and Mathis kept looking at the empty chairs more than the full ones. He had invited eleven people. Nine had come. Tristen was already halfway through her second Shirley Temple, toasting no one in particular, and Kody was stacking creamers into a tower that would not survive the appetizers.

"You're doing the face," Tristen said, pointing her straw at him. "The graduation-program face. You did it all through the ceremony, in the gym, when they read the names."

"Because they skipped some names," Mathis said. "Or people skipped the ceremony. I don't know which."

Mr. Villanueva, who had taught them junior English and had shown up with a card for each of them, leaned back in his chair with the unhurried patience of a man who had watched a lot of classes pass through. "Counting again," he said, but he said it lightly, and he didn't offer anything else, which Mathis had learned was his way of leaving a door open rather than closing one.

Mathis had spent the afternoon before the ceremony doing something he was slightly embarrassed to admit: he'd looked up the numbers. Not for a class, not for an assignment. He'd been trying to find Derek Ruiz on social media, and then Marcus, and then a girl named Alyssa who had sat behind him in algebra freshman year, and none of them had walked across the stage that morning, and he'd wanted to know if that was normal or if his grade was cursed. The national average adjusted cohort graduation rate for public high school students was 87 percent in the 2021-22 school year. He'd read the sentence four times. Eighty-seven percent of students who started ninth grade together got to this day, and thirteen percent didn't, and he had never once thought about the thirteen percent until he was standing in the middle of the eighty-seven.

"I found a statistic," he said now, because Tristen had asked him twice what he was staring at. "The national rate. It's eighty-seven percent. For 2021-22, public schools, adjusted cohort graduation rate, whatever that means exactly. It counts everyone who started ninth grade with us." He'd already learned the hard part of the term from the website's own fine print, the way a whole cohort gets followed for four years, and he didn't want to lecture, so he just said, "Thirteen out of a hundred didn't walk today."

Kody's tower of creamers wobbled and held. "So statistically we're the lucky ones," he said. "Great. Can we order now?"

"It's not luck," Tristen said, and there was an edge in it that hadn't been at her birthday party in March. She turned her glass slowly by its rim. "My cousin should be here. He started ninth grade the same year we did, same building, and nobody from the school called after he stopped showing up. Nobody called for months. So when you say eighty-seven percent like it's the weather, like it just happens, that's not how it lands." She looked up. "That's not a criticism of you. I'm just saying it's a number made out of people."

Mathis sat with that. He had, he admitted to himself, been treating the statistic two ways at once, and both ways felt dishonest the moment she said that. One was the cerebral way, the way Mr. Villanueva had taught them to read a poem, holding the thing at a distance, noting its shape. The other was the Derek way: a kid who had moved twice sophomore year and then just stopped answering texts. He had been switching between the two without noticing, and Tristen had caught him mid-switch. Maybe the honest position was holding both at once and admitting they didn't fit together neatly. The number was true, and the number was made out of people, and he didn't have to choose, but he did have to carry both or he was lying about one of them.

"Fair," he said. "Both things." Then, because Kody was signaling the waiter with the desperation of a starving man, "Also I want to text Derek. Tonight, not someday. He's still in the city."

"He might not answer," Kody said, not unkindly, finally letting the creamers fall with a small clatter. "Honestly? Half of what you say to people who left is for you, not them. It's like you want the verisimilitude of caring, the look of it, without the awkward actual conversation."

"That's brutal," Mathis said.

"That's Kody," Tristen said, and for a second the table laughed, and Mr. Villanueva raised his water glass as if toasting the accuracy of it, which did not presage a rescue. He was clearly enjoying the argument too much to end it.

When the food came, they talked about dorms and roommates and the meal plan Tristen called a scam, and the conversation moved on the way conversations do, and Mathis let it move. But under the table his phone was in his hand, and he had typed half a message to Derek, deleted it, typed it again: congratulations would be wrong, sorry would be worse. He settled on "saw the stage today and thought of you, no pressure, just saying." He looked at it for a long moment while Tristen argued with Kody about whether the town's new burrito place was actually any good. Then, before he could overthink it further, before the waiter cleared their plates, he pressed send and set the phone face-up beside his water glass, where he could see it.

He was carrying his box of leftovers out to the parking lot, Kody and Tristen arguing ahead of him about music for the drive, when the phone buzzed in his jacket pocket. He stopped under the restaurant's lit sign and looked at the screen. "Yeah," Derek had written. "good for you man. you free friday?" Mathis stood there a second longer, the box warm against his ribs, then typed, "friday works," and walked to catch up with his friends.

activity: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
knowledge_domain: terms related to responsibility, trade-offs and unintended consequences used in structured ethical reasoning
fact: Sociologist Robert K. Merton's 1936 essay 'The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action' listed causes of unintended consequences, including ignorance, error and focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones.
story:
The proposal had seemed airtight in the library at lunch, when Samuel spread the numbers across the table and Kinsley leaned over them with her chin in her hand. The cafeteria was throwing out forty trays of untouched food a day, most of it the pre-portioned fruit and the bread that came with every hot lunch. If the council got the cafeteria to switch to an opt-in system, students would take only what they wanted, and the waste would drop. Blaine had already made the poster, a photo of a overflowing garbage bin with the word WHY? across it in red. Samuel could almost feel the meeting where they would present it, the way the principal would nod.

They got the nod. Ms. Flores, who supervised council and taught civics down in the portables, signed off with only one caution, delivered while watering the ferns on her windowsill. "Plans are easy," she said. "Consequences are the part that doesn't ask your permission." Samuel had written it in the margin of his notebook because it sounded like something a poster should say.

For two weeks it worked. The kitchen staff reported the waste down by more than half, and Blaine taped the chart to the cafeteria door so everyone could watch the line sink. Then the nurse began sending home letters. Then Samuel noticed the boy from his chemistry class, the quiet one who always took two milks, now taking none. Then Kinsley found him after fourth period, standing by the gym doors with her phone held out. "Marcus's mom called the office," she said. "He's been skipping dinner at home because he's on the free lunch plan, and under opt-in he wasn't taking the full tray anymore. He thought taking less was the point." The fruit and bread nobody wanted had been the part somebody did want, and the opt-in form required a signature some parents never sent back. The plan that fed the landfill less had fed a boy less too.

At the emergency council meeting, Ms. Flores did not lecture them. She asked one question and then sat down. "Why didn't any of you see it coming?" The room was quiet enough to hear the radiator tick. Blaine said nobody could have known, but Samuel, staring at the chart on the door, its proud descending line, did not believe that, and neither, he suspected, did she.

That night he searched the phrase on his laptop, following links through a university site until he landed on an essay from 1936 by a sociologist named Robert K. Merton, called "The Unanticipated Consequences of Purposive Social Action." He read it twice at the kitchen table while his mother drained pasta behind him. Merton had actually listed causes of unintended consequences: ignorance, error, and the habit of focusing on immediate interests over long-term ones. Samuel copied the three into his notebook, then sat looking at them. Which one were they? They had not been ignorant about hunger in the school, exactly; they had known Marcus existed, had even voted last year on a breakfast program. They had not made an error in the arithmetic. What they had done was care intensely about the chart, about the red poster, about the feeling of having fixed something by Friday. He thought of the way he and Kinsley had titrated the plan down to its most presentable form, trimming every complication that would have slowed the vote, and how the trimmed parts had been exactly the ones that bit.

The next morning he told Kinsley in the stairwell, holding his notebook open between them. "It's a thing," he said. "Unanticipated consequences. This guy Merton wrote about it in 1936. Ignorance, error, or caring about the short term more than the long term." She read it, then looked up. "So which were we?" "The third one," Samuel said. "We knew hunger was here. It wasn't autochthonous to some other school. It was ours and we looked past it because the chart went down." She didn't argue, which was worse than if she had.

They brought a revision to the council: keep opt-in but make the fruit and bread a take-home table anyone could use without a form, no questions, no names. It passed, and Blaine volunteered to staff it Tuesdays. The waste line on the chart ticked back up, not to where it started, but up, and Samuel felt the strange double weight of that, the gain and the cost sitting in the same hand.

On the first Thursday of the new table, Samuel stayed after to carry the leftover apples to the bin that went to the shelter, and found Marcus there already, filling his backpack, unhurried, like a small epicure selecting from a limited menu. Samuel almost said something about the plan, about Merton, about the whole machinery of it. Instead he picked up an apple himself and polished it on his sleeve. "They're the good ones today," Marcus said.

"That's because nobody wanted them," Samuel said, and took a bite.

activity: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
knowledge_domain: the idea that historians disagree about the past because sources are partial and questions change
fact: Historiography is the study of how history has been written, including how historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time.
story:
On the Monday after the unit test, Ms. Tanaka set a shoebox on the front desk and said nothing about it, which Jack found more theatrical than informative. He had his own problem to think about anyway: his essay on the Korean War had come back with a B and a single comment in the margin, "Whose version?" He wanted the A, and more than the A he wanted the answer, because until Friday he had assumed there was one.

The box, when she finally opened it, held old textbooks. She passed them down the rows and told them to look at the chapter on the war, then compare it with the chapter in their own books, the ones still warm from their bags. Jack got a copy with a cracked spine and a name written inside the cover in careful cursive, and next to the name, a date that made him do the subtraction twice.

"Whose version is right?" Jazmine asked from the window row, and Ms. Tanaka said, "I'm not going to tell you," which Jack thought was an evasion until he realized it was the assignment.

Damon, two seats over, was already leafing through with the sardonic expression he wore when he thought a class was being staged around him. "They're going to tell us the books disagree," he said, not quite under his voice. "Big surprise. Everything disagrees if you go back far enough."

Jack read. In the old book the war began in a paragraph of four sentences, each of them confident, and in his own book the same beginning took two pages and still seemed to hedge, weighing one set of documents against another. He looked for the moment the accounts split, and found it earlier than he expected, not in the events but in the questions the books seemed to be answering. The old book asked what happened. His book asked, underneath everything, how anyone knew.

"That's my grandmother's book," Jazmine said suddenly, and Jack looked up. She was holding her copy toward the light, pointing at the name inside the cover. "This is her name. Ms. Tanaka asked her to lend it." The room went quiet in the way rooms do when a private fact surfaces in a public place. Jazmine said that when she'd visited in August, her grandmother had told the story of the war differently from any book, with an uncle in it, and a winter that no chapter measured.

By happenstance Jack's copy was from the same printing, the same edition, and he told her so, and then found he had nothing to add. He had been hunting for the correct version all week, and now he was sitting in a room with three of them, one of them a woman's voice he had never heard.

"There's a word for this," Ms. Tanaka said, and Jack, who had found it two nights ago while rewriting his essay and had underlined it twice, said it before she could. "Historiography." She raised an eyebrow, neither praise nor correction, and wrote it on the board. Jack kept going, because the sentence had been building in him since the margin comment. "It's the study of how history has been written. How historians' interpretations of the same events have changed over time." Saying it aloud made it sound smaller and larger at once, like handing someone a key without the door.

"You're just saying nobody knows anything," Damon said.

"I'm not." Jack turned the old textbook over in his hands. "I'm saying the old book wasn't lying. It answered the questions its readers were asking. The questions changed, so the history changed. That's not nothing knowing, that's knowing how the knowing got made." It came out clumsier than he'd drafted it, and he could feel his ears going warm.

Jazmine was copying the chapter's first paragraph onto a notecard, interpolating nothing, she said, wanting her grandmother's words exact, though she admitted she couldn't check them until Thanksgiving. Jack watched her write and understood that his essay would have to end differently than he'd planned, not with the answer but with the three versions laid side by side and an honest paragraph about what he still couldn't settle: whether his own book would look cracked-spined and confident to some student fifty years on.

He raised his hand to ask if he could rewrite for a new grade, and Ms. Tanaka said he could rewrite regardless, the grade was the least of it. At the door, Jazmine caught his sleeve. "Ask her about the uncle," she said. "When I get the recording. You can put it in your essay."

"Put what in?" Damon called from down the hall. "There's no ending yet."

"Exactly," Jack said, and held the old textbook a moment longer before handing it back.

activity: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
knowledge_domain: how a bill becomes a law through drafting, committee review, debate, votes and assent
fact: Under the US Constitution, if the president neither signs nor vetoes a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress is in session, it becomes law without a signature.
story:
Tristan had claimed the study room at the public library for three consecutive Saturdays, and Cynthia had begun to treat this as a personal insult. "You know it's the only room with a whiteboard," she said, dropping her bag on the table anyway. "The anime club has rights too. We were here first in spirit."

"In spirit doesn't enfranchise you," Tristan said, not looking up from his laptop. "Actual reservations enfranchise you. I have one." Cynthia rolled her eyes, but she sat down across from him and started unpacking her辩论 materials, because her real want, she admitted, was his opinion on her opening argument for the regional debate tournament, where the resolution concerned whether citizens' assemblies were better than legislatures. She needed a devil's advocate. Tristan was constitutionally incapable of being anything else.

His own problem was more urgent. The school paper had assigned him a piece on a bill in Congress, the one about requiring colleges to publish the true total cost of attendance before students committed. His older sister had been ambushed by fees two years ago, and Tristan had tracked the bill through its whole life online: the initial draft, which read like someone's rough homework; the committee markup, where a sentence about textbook costs got added and a sentence about meal plans got cut; the floor debate, where one senator called the whole thing "aCosmopolitan fantasy of bureaucratic kindness," whatever that meant; and the votes, 68 to 32 in one chamber, then a compromise version in the other, then the compromise again in the first. He had written half his article around the final moment. The president, his draft said, had refused to sign the bill, and in doing so had killed it, "a quiet pocket veto for a quieter betrayal."

Peyton arrived at noon with two coffees and read the draft over Tristan's shoulder, the way Peyton did everything, uninvited and usually correctly. "Your lede's wrong," Peyton said. "It passed. It's law. It went into effect this week."

"That's impossible. He never signed it. There's no record of a signature anywhere on the tracker."

"Then check the Constitution instead of the tracker," Peyton said, and went back to Cynthia's note cards, because Peyton believed every argument should be tested to destruction and thought Cynthia's hook about ancient Athens was, quote, "an artifice to avoid talking about modern voters."

Tristan walked into the stacks and found the volume, and there it was in Article I, in language so dry it felt like a dare. If the president neither signed nor vetoed a bill within ten days, Sundays excepted, while Congress was in session, the bill became law without a signature. He read it twice. The bill had sat on the president's desk through the whole span of days, Sundays excluded from the count, and Congress had never adjourned, and so a law had come into being out of pure silence. Not a refusal, he realized. Not a betrayal. Something stranger: an abstention that still counted as a yes.

He came back to the table and started cutting his second paragraph. Cynthia leaned over. "What did you find?"

"That silence can pass a law," Tristan said. "If Congress is still in session, the president ignoring a bill for ten days, not counting Sundays, makes it law anyway. No signature at all."

"So your whole column was a lie?"

"It was wrong, which is different." He typed while he talked, rebuilding the piece around the truth, which was harder to write and better. His sister's fees still mattered, the bill still mattered, but the story was no longer about a villain. It was about a system built to keep moving even when someone at the top declined to move, and about a guy at a library table who had assumed inaction meant death because that was the simpler sentence.

Mr. Singh passed by with the cart of returns and paused at Tristan's screen. "Third Saturday on this one," he said. "Is it winning?"

"It passed," Tristan said. "Nobody signed it, and it passed anyway."

"Good," Mr. Singh said, pushing the cart on. "The whiteboard is free at four, if the anime club still wants it."

Cynthia wrote her name on the sign-up sheet before Tristan could even close his laptop.

activity: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
knowledge_domain: how interest makes borrowed money cost more over time and makes savings grow
fact: The US Consumer Financial Protection Bureau notes a typical payday loan fee of $15 per $100 borrowed for two weeks equals an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent.
story:
The flyer had been taped to the lamp post outside school all week, and by Thursday Abigail could recite it without looking: fast cash, no credit check, two weeks. She was still thinking about it in fifth period, where Mr. Nur was returning their essays on interpretation, when she noticed Haroon hadn't picked his up. He sat with his hands flat on the desk, and when the bell rang he was first out the door.

She caught him at his locker. "You failed the hermeneutics paper?"

"I didn't turn it in." He shut the locker harder than the latch required. "It's my mom's rent. I'm three hundred short by Monday, and my check doesn't come till the fifteenth."

"The one on Delancey," she said, meaning the flyer. "The lamp post one."

"Fifteen dollars per hundred. The guy at the counter said it's just a fee, not even interest, really."

Abigail pulled a pen from her bag and flattened a napkin on top of his locker. She wrote 15/100 and then, underneath, the way her mother made her do unit rates before she'd let her buy anything on sale. Fifteen per hundred, every two weeks. There were fifty-two weeks in a year, twenty-six two-week stretches, and she multiplied it out twice because the first answer looked wrong. It wasn't wrong. Compounded the same way, a typical fee like that came to an annual percentage rate of almost 400 percent.

"That can't be right." Haroon leaned over the napkin.

"Do it yourself." She slid him the pen. "Three hundred means forty-five dollars in two weeks. But if you can't pay it back in two weeks, you roll it. That's forty-five again. And again."
