He did the arithmetic with his lips moving, and then he stood very still, holding the pen the way you hold something when you've decided not to throw it. Daria appeared beside them with her saxophone case and read the napkin upside down. "Mr. Nur's been trying to get people to save since September," she said. "He keeps saying interest works for you if you give it time."

"That's the weird part," Abigail said. She was thinking of the savings account her grandmother had opened when Abigail was nine, twenty dollars a month, which she'd always considered a kind of joke until she'd logged in last spring and found it had grown past everything her grandmother had put in. The money had done work on its own, quietly, while she'd been ignoring it. The same force, she understood now, ran both directions, and the lamp post people had simply aimed it the other way.

"So what do I do," Haroon said. It came out flat, not a question so much as something set down between them.

"You could ask your landlord for four days."

"He charges late fees. He's not a person who negotiates."

"You're going to litigate with a loan shark instead? Forty-five dollars, then ninety, then a hundred and thirty-five, that's your negotiation."

Daria shifted her case to the other hand. "My mom's in the office till six. She'd float you three hundred, no fee."

Haroon looked at the napkin again, then folded it in half and put it in his pocket, which Abigail chose to read as him keeping the numbers rather than hiding them. "I'd pay her back on the fifteenth," he said. "Both of you know that."

"Then tell her that," Daria said.

They walked out through the double doors together, and on the corner of Delancey the lamp post still carried its flyer, though someone had torn the bottom phone number strip into confetti, mostly. Abigail stood in front of it while the other two waited at the crosswalk. She thought about her grandmother's account earning whatever small percentage it earned, patient, invisible, and about the almost 400 percent waiting inside that cheerful blue sign, and she could not have said which she found more frightening, except that one of them had been on her side all along.

She took out the pen, crossed out FFAST CASH, and wrote over it in small letters: do the math. Then she ran to catch up.

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: In Chicago, MLA and APA styles, entries in the final list of sources are arranged alphabetically by the author's surname, not in the order the sources were cited.
story:
Oliver had claimed the corner table by the window on the second floor of the public library, the one with the wobbly leg that everyone else avoided, because the wobble was worth the light. Spread before him were six books, three printed articles, a stack of index cards, and a style guide he'd checked out that morning. His thesis, typed at the top of a blank document, read that the city's decision to sell its public water utility had been defensible in 1994 and indefensible now, and he had spent two days assembling evidence that refused to line up behind either half of that sentence.

The paper was for Ms. Zhao's class, though she also worked Saturdays at the reference desk downstairs, which meant Oliver saw his teacher on weekends in a cardigan instead of a blazer, stamping returned books with a laconic efficiency that made him feel she was judging his overdue fines as she judged his essays. She had assigned the paper with a warning that still stung: an argument is not a pile of quotations with your name at the top. He suspected she had said it while looking at him, though he could not prove it, and he had not asked.

He had, however, texted Nico, who had written a research paper the previous semester and spoken about it since with the solemnity of a survivor. Nico's reply came while Oliver was sorting his index cards into something resembling an order.

"You need a system," the message read. "Mine was: every quote gets a card, every card gets a footnote, and the whole thing builds toward the last source being the one that knocks down the other side. Like a closing argument. Also bring snacks tomorrow because the vending machine took my dollar and I hold the library partly responsible. I've been drafting a complaint. It's two sentences."

Oliver smiled at the phrase partly responsible, which was more diplomacy than he would have managed. He wrote back that he would bring snacks and that his own system was less like a closing argument and more like a hostage negotiation between six authors who despised each other. The engineer's report blamed the city council. The council's minutes blamed the federal mandate. A newspaper columnist from 1995 blamed everybody, in prose Oliver admired and could not cite, because admiration was not evidence.

He worked until the light moved off the table and onto the carpet. When he finally built his list of sources, he did what felt natural: he entered them in the order he had used them, since that order felt like the shape of his thinking, a trail a reader could follow from his first tentative claim to his last. The engineer came first because the engineer had come first.

The next afternoon Nico arrived with a highlighter behind each ear and read the draft while Oliver pretended to read the style guide. On the last page Nico stopped tapping his foot.

"You listed these backwards," Nico said.

"They're in the order I cited them."

"Right, but that's not how it works. In Chicago, MLA and APA, the final list goes alphabetically by the author's surname. Not the order you used them."

Oliver looked at his list, then at the style guide, then at his list again. He found the section, ran a finger down it, and confirmed it. The author whose argument had arrived last in his thinking, the council apologist named Aldous Brennan, would now appear first on the page, above the engineer whose report had started everything.

He spent a strange ten minutes rearranging entries, and the strangeness was not the alphabet. It was that the new order told a different story. Brennan first, then the columnist, then the engineer buried in the middle, his thunderclap of a report reduced to one voice among six, alphabetically equal to everyone it had accused. Oliver sat back and let the two versions sit side by side in his head, the trail of his thinking and the flat, democratic order the styles demanded, and could not decide which one was more honest.

He went downstairs to test the question on the only adult who might adjudicate it without grading him. Ms. Zhao was shelving holds, and she listened with her arms full of paperbacks.

"So it's alphabetical no matter what," Oliver said. "Even if the order I cited them in means something."

"It means something to you," she said. "Put the citation order in your head, not on the page." She slid a paperback into its slot without looking at it. "Then write a paragraph telling me why the engineer is wrong, if he is. That's where order matters. Your order."

He wanted to ask her whether the engineer was wrong, whether the council deserved the culpability the report assigned them or whether the whole thing had been a trap built decades before anyone now living had voted on it, but he had learned that Ms. Zhao answered those questions with questions, and he had only so much vacation left. He carried the ambiguity back upstairs like a second stack of books.

In his conclusion, drafted that evening under the window while the lights of the parking lot came on, Oliver kept his claim but softened its joints. The sale had been defensible given what the council knew, indefensible given what it declined to know, and he footnoted both halves, and his bibliography ran alphabetically, Aldous Brennan presiding over a page of witnesses who did not agree with him and did not have to. Nico read it, removed one highlighter from behind his ear, and pointed it at the final paragraph without saying anything, which in Nico's language was a standing ovation.

"He's still first," Oliver said, nodding at the bibliography.

"Alphabetically," Nico said, and took the last of the snacks.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Earthenware pottery is normally fired below about 1,200 degrees Celsius, while porcelain is fired between about 1,200 and 1,400 degrees Celsius.
story:
Leah spread the newspaper across the kitchen table and set the two clay bowls side by side, hers the dull red-brown of earthenware, Sofie's a pale grey that would turn white when it was finished. Her mother had gone to bed early, so the house was quiet except for the refrigerator's hum, and Leah had the table to herself, which was the reprieve she'd been waiting for all week. She ran a thumb along the rim of her bowl, feeling the roughness of it, and thought about the note Sofie had left folded inside her locker that afternoon.

"Ask Ms. Hernández if we can fire together," Sofie had written in her cramped, hurried hand. "I checked and I think it works. Also your bowl is better than mine and you should stop saying it isn't. Bring my glaze Tuesday." The last sentence had a line under it, twice. Leah had read the note four times during physics, once during lunch, and again now, holding it between two fingers above the table like evidence in a trial she was conducting against herself.

She had not wanted to take the pottery class at first. That had been her decision, back in September, to sign up for economics instead, something practical, something that would look organised on a college application. Then she had watched Kian carry a lopsided mug out of Ms. Hernández's room in October, grinning like he'd invented the concept of a handle, and she had changed her schedule the next morning. Her mother had asked if she was sure. Leah had said yes, and she had meant it, but she'd also spent three months half-expecting someone to tell her the switch had been a mistake, that wanting to make things with her hands was not a serious way to spend her last year of school.

Tuesday afternoon the studio smelled like wet dust and lemon soap, and the kiln room was warm enough that Leah's glasses fogged as she acclimated to it. Ms. Hernández was loading the first kiln of the week, stacking shelves with practised, unhurried movements, and Sofie was already there, obstreperous as ever, arguing that her porcelain test tiles deserved the best spot in the chamber.

"Put mine in the back," Leah said, setting her bowl on the loading cart. "Wherever it fits."

Sofie stopped mid-sentence. "Leah. They can't go in the same load."

"They can't what?"

"Ms. Hernández told us in September. Earthenware fires below about twelve hundred degrees, and porcelain needs between about twelve hundred and fourteen hundred." Sofie said it the way she recited chemistry equations, flat and certain, then softened. "Yours would crack, or mine wouldn't vitrify. I don't actually know which. I just know it's wrong."

Leah looked at her bowl, then at the pale grey tiles Sofie was protecting like eggs. She had been so pleased with her piece, so quietly certain it belonged near the centre of things, and now the physics of heat itself had divided them. "Different loads," she said slowly, testing the idea. "So mine goes in the low-fire batch, and yours waits for the hot one. Two firings. Two schedules."

"Two schedules," Sofie agreed, and Ms. Hernández, without turning from the kiln, said, "Now you know why the schedule on the door has two columns." She lifted Leah's bowl and placed it on the lower shelf herself, careful with it, and something in the gentleness of that gesture made Leah's throat tighten unexpectedly.

They stayed until the studio closed, Sofie sketching ideas for the porcelain load and Leah wrapping her fired, cooled bowl three days later in a scarf to carry home. Walking through the cold parking lot, she held the package against her chest and thought that the economics class would have met at this hour, in a room with a projector and no dust, and that she would have learned something true and useful there too. Both things could be true. The clay needed one temperature and the porcelain needed another, and neither was a lesser material, and she could not yet say whether the person she was becoming in this room was the person she had meant to become. She unlocked the front door, set the bowl on the kitchen table where the newspaper still lay, and peeled back the scarf to look at it under the overhead light.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: The US National Safety Council recommends a following distance of at least three seconds, adding a second for each difficulty such as bad weather or heavy traffic.
story:
The permit had lived in Connor's wallet for eight months, and his father had finally run out of ways to postpone the Saturday lesson, because the road test was scheduled for Thursday and the state required supervised hours that Connor did not yet have. The car was his mother's, a sedan with a spartan interior, cloth seats and a radio that only worked if you thumped the dashboard twice, and it sat in the driveway on the quiet suburban street like an animal that had decided to tolerate him.

"One thing before you touch anything," his father said, settling into the passenger seat with the air of a man bracing for turbulence. "Following distance. Three seconds. That's the number from the National Safety Council, and it's a minimum."

Connor repeated it to be agreeate. He had already heard the opposite, though, and loudly, from Juan, who had passed his test in June and had lambasted the three-second rule over lunch with the confidence of someone who had been driving for a hundred and eleven days. "Two seconds," Juan had insisted, tapping the table. "Three is for grandmas. My cousin's a cop and he says two." Connor had nodded then the way you nod at things you don't intend to obey, but now, with the wheel actually in his hands, the numbers had started to matter.

He pulled out of the driveway and drove the loop of their street at a speed that would have embarrassed a mail truck. His father made him do it twice more, and on the third pass the neighbor's dog, a beagle of some indefatigable genus that had spent years perfecting the art of darting out at cars, streaked across the road ahead. Connor braked hard enough that their seatbelts caught them both, and the beagle made it to the other side without breaking stride, and nobody said anything for the length of the whole block.

"That's why it's three seconds," his father said finally. Connor started to answer, started to defend two, and then thought about the beagle and kept his mouth shut. That night he texted Juan anyway, because it seemed unfair to surrender an argument without evidence. Juan sent back a shrug emoji and the word "grandma." So Connor did what he should have done before arguing at lunch: he looked it up himself. The National Safety Council said at least three seconds, and it said more than that. You added a second for each difficulty, one for bad weather, one for heavy traffic, and the picture that emerged was not a fixed rule at all but a kind of arithmetic, distance as something you calculated fresh every time the road changed. Juan's two seconds wasn't just wrong, it was wrong in a way Connor had been wrong too, thinking the answer was a single number somebody could hand you.

The next morning it rained, a thin persistent drizzle that put a shine on everything, and his father appeared at Connor's bedroom door holding the car keys. "Weather counts as a difficulty," he said. "Do the math yourself." They drove the same loop and then, when Connor held his nerve, out through the subdivision to the road with the light traffic and the long gentle hill. Connor counted in his head at the mailbox, one-two-three-four, watching the taillights of the car ahead, holding a gap that felt enormous and looked, in the mirror, like nothing at all. When a truck swung out of the depot lot ahead of them, he had the whole four seconds to ease off the gas instead of stomping the brake, and his father said nothing, which was its own kind of language.

The problem, as far as Connor could tell, was that Juan wasn't an idiot, and neither was the National Safety Council, and the gap between two seconds and four seconds was the gap between two ways of being in the world, one that trusted your reflexes and one that trusted the possibility that a beagle would appear. He didn't think he could fully close that gap before Thursday, or maybe ever. What he had was a method: count, adjust, count again, and accept that the right distance on a dry street would be wrong in the rain.

Thursday came gray and then cleared. Connor sat in the waiting line at the testing center with the window down, the examiner's clipboard balanced on her knee like a verdict waiting to be written. At the first stop sign, a car he hadn't seen came through the intersection late, and Connor, who was already counting, watched it pass and let the silence stretch to a full three seconds before he touched the gas. The examiner made a small mark on her clipboard, and Connor drove on into the street.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Condoms are the only common contraceptive method that also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections.
story:
Nolan locked the stall door in the third-floor bathroom and took out the index cards, though he already knew he would not look at them. Ms. O'Brien had asked him on Tuesday, in the flat tone she used for favors she expected to be refused, whether he would run the peer health session for the ninth graders on Friday. Consent, contraception, and how to get tested at the clinic on Marsh Street. He had said yes before he understood what yes would require, which was standing in a bathroom on Thursday afternoon, saying the words out loud to a metal door.

"Consent," he began, "is a freely given, reversible, informed, enthusiastic, specific yes." He had learned the acronym and hated it a little, the way the letters made something careful seem like a slogan. Still, the door was an indifferent audience, its grey paint chipped around the latch, and he kept going. "You can say yes to one thing and no to another. You can change your mind halfway. If someone's drunk, it's not consent."

The outer door banged open and Colin came in fast, sneakers squeaking, and dropped onto the counter by the sinks. "Nolan? You in here?"

Nolan stayed quiet a moment, then flushed the toilet for cover and came out washing his hands. "Rehearsing."

"For the ninth graders." Colin nodded, but his attention was somewhere else, jittering. Colin, who normally wanted to monetize everything, who had once tried to sell playlists of study sounds to sophomores at three dollars a download, looked like a person who wanted something he couldn't price. "I need to ask you something," he said. "About the clinic thing. Marsh Street."

Nolan leaned on the sink. "You can just go. You don't need a reason or a parent. You walk in, you ask for testing, they take a sample, they call you in a week."

"Is it, like, anonymous?" Colin was studying the impermeable surface of the mirror as though it might answer for him.

"They assign you a number if you want. Yeah."

The summer before, Nolan remembered, he had stood in the pharmacy on Cord Avenue while Kellen picked up her prescription. She was a year older, brisk about most things, mortified about this one, and she had asked the pharmacist, her voice pitched low, whether the pill she'd just paid for also protected against infections. The pharmacist had shaken her head, kind and unembarrassed, and said that condoms were the only common contraceptive method that also reduced that risk. Kellen had stood very still holding the paper bag, and then said, "Good to know," in a voice that made Nolan understand she hadn't known, that whole months of her life had rested on a wrong idea. She'd thanked him afterward for coming along, and he'd never asked what she did with the information. He was still a little ashamed of how relieved he'd been not to ask.

"You should put that in your session," Colin said now, reading his face like a poster. "The pharmacist thing. Half those kids think the pill covers everything." He hesitated, drumming his heels against the cabinet. "I told Dara we didn't need anything. Last month. And I believed it, mostly, and then Kellen said something at lunch about her cousin, and now I don't know what I believe."

Nolan looked at his index cards, at the blank backs of them. "The clinic does walk-ins until five," he said. "I can come with you. Not inside. Or inside, if you want. Whatever you want."

"That's the thing you're supposed to say, right? The consent thing." Colin half-laughed. "You're rehearsing on me."

"It's the same principle. It works or it doesn't depending on whether you mean it." Nolan heard how that sounded, like artifice wearing the costume of sincerity, and pushed past it. "I mean it."

The bell above the hallway speaker gave its first warning ring. Colin slid off the counter and stood there, bag strap twisted in both hands, not moving toward the door.

"Friday," Nolan said, "when I'm up there with the ninth graders, somebody's going to be sitting in the back row who needs it and won't ask. You were going to be that kid in the back row for two more months, maybe." He stopped, because he'd started lecturing, and Ms. O'Brien had told him the fastest way to lose a room was to sound like you already knew everything. There was plenty he didn't know, including what Kellen had decided, including what Colin would do with the next hour.

Colin pulled the strap straight and looked at the door. "Until five, you said."

"Until five," Nolan said, and picked up his cards.

activity: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
knowledge_domain: to compare how a parliamentary and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government
fact: In 2022 the United Kingdom had three prime ministers, Boris Johnson, Liz Truss and Rishi Sunak, without a general election, because the governing party changed its leader.
story:
The summons had arrived three weeks after his eighteenth birthday, as if the county had been waiting for him to become eligible, and so Simon spent the first morning of his summer inside a courthouse annex with bad fluorescent lighting and a comparative politics textbook on his knees. The makeup exam was in six days. He was meant to be comparing how a parliamentary system and a presidential system choose and remove a head of government, and instead he was watching a woman in a gray cardigan read names from a clipboard.

"Simon Kessler," the woman said. "Juror four." Anita, two rows ahead of him, turned around and mouthed jury five with obvious delight. They had been in the same government class until Ms. Becker had flagged them both for the departmental exam they had missed during the quarantine week, and here they were, summoned to the same panel, which felt less like coincidence than like the county demonstrating a concept.

The case, when it finally began after two hours of voir dire, was a civil dispute between a homeowners' association and its former president, a man named only in the papers as the defendant, who had been removed from his position at a special meeting and now claimed the removal was improper. The judge gave the jury a set of instructions, one of which contained the word injunction, defined by nothing she said afterward, since she assumed they knew; Simon wrote it in the margin of his notebook anyway, next to a half-finished sentence about votes of no confidence.

During the first recess, in the hallway with the water fountain that burped, Anita showed him her phone. Her aunt and cousins lived outside Manchester, and she had been ruminating on something they had told her all through the spring. "In 2022 the UK had three prime ministers in one year," she said. "Boris Johnson, then Liz Truss, then Rishi Sunak. No general election the whole time. My cousin watched Truss go in and out like she was trying on coats."

"That can't be right," Simon said. "You can't just swap heads of government. There'd have to be a vote."

"That's what I said. But the governing party changed its leader, and the leader's the prime minister, so. Three of them." She shrugged, the way she shrugged at anything that came from her aunt, whom she suspected of exaggerating even when she wasn't.

In the jury room the next day, Simon was elected foreman because he was sitting nearest the door when the marshal asked if they had chosen, and nobody wanted to volunteer. The deliberation went badly from the start. Four jurors thought the board had followed its bylaws; four thought the special meeting hadn't been noticed properly; the last three, including Anita, kept raising what the foreman of the previous day, a retired schoolteacher, called ancillary concerns, like whether the defendant had been rude at the meeting, which was not in evidence and not in the instructions. Simon tried to manage it. He summarized, he polled, he drew a diagram of the timeline on a napkin, and by mid-afternoon he realized he had stopped listening to the arguments and started listening only for whether they were moving.

On the second morning of deliberations, the retired schoolteacher suggested, in a mild and terrible voice, that maybe the problem was the foreman. "No offense, sweetheart," she said, which was offense. "But we've gone around the circle four times and we're exactly where we started." There was no rule against it, the marshal confirmed through the door; the jury could choose its own foreman. They voted, and Simon watched his own hands rise to abstain, and the count was nine to remove him. Anita kept her hand down, but she didn't say anything, and Anita was appointed in his place because she had the notebook with everyone's names in it.

He sat with it for an hour, being an ordinary juror again, and found that it loosened something. Without the responsibility of moving them, he could hear them. The schoolteacher's objection wasn't about him; she wanted a verdict before her parking expired. The man in the Carhartt jacket kept saying "elected" when he meant "chosen," and when Simon finally understood that, he understood the whole disagreement. Half the room thought being president of the association was an office you held until the members voted you out, and half thought it was a role the board gave and could take away, and the bylaws, badly drafted, supported both readings at once.

It was the same knot as his exam. He had been ruminating on Anita's three prime ministers for two days, and now the jury room made it concrete. A parliamentary system could change its leader the way this board had changed its president, internally, without asking the wider membership, and whether that was a defect or a feature depended entirely on what you thought the leader was for. He wasn't sure yet. He wrote in the margin, next to injunction, that both systems could remove, and neither made removal painless, and that the honest answer to the exam question probably ended in a paragraph he couldn't write until he knew what he thought fairness required of a majority.

At four o'clock they reached a verdict, seven to five, that the removal had been proper, and Simon voted with the five. Anita read the form aloud in the courtroom, steady and clear, and the judge thanked them, and outside on the courthouse steps the light was the long gold kind. "You're not still mad," she said. It wasn't quite a question.

"I was never mad," he said, which was not true, and then, more honestly: "I learned more being fired than being foreman."

Anita laughed and held up her phone, a text from her cousin glowing on the screen: ask Simon if he knows how many PMs we had in 2022.

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: In Java, 'this.name = name' uses the keyword 'this' to mean the object's own field when a parameter has the same name.
story:
Hannah had agreed to come to Guneet's basement on the understanding that they would study for the computer science placement test, and by study Guneet apparently meant sit on a beanbag chair eating pretzels while Marko hogged the actual keyboard. The basement smelled like laundry detergent and old carpet, and a lamp with a cracked shade made the whole room the color of weak tea. On the screen was an empty file called Student.java, which Marko had been staring at for ten minutes as though it might fill itself.

"You're supposed to write a class," Hannah said. "Private fields. Getters. Then test it." She had the assignment sheet folded in her back pocket, softened from being sat on.

"I'm prognosticating," Marko said. "I'm envisioning the architecture."

"You're stalling."

He typed while Guneet watched over his shoulder, chewing. The class took shape: private String name; private int age; then a constructor Marko slapped together in eight seconds. When he ran the test file he had written, the output printed a row of nulls where the names should have been. Guneet leaned in, squinting, and offered the opinion that the computer was broken. Marko declared Java a scam invented to torment first-year students. Hannah pulled the desk chair over and sat down between them.

"Run it again," she said, though she knew it would print the same thing, because it had printed the same thing, and computers were impervious to hoping. She read the constructor line by line. The parameters were named name and age, which was sensible and tidy, and the body said name = name; and age = age; and she could see that it looked right, which was the problem, because it wasn't. She had read something about this at two in the morning, half asleep, in a forum thread where everyone argued about naming conventions instead of answering the question. She'd dismissed the thread then. Now she closed her eyes and tried to recall it.

"Wait," she said. "I think the parameter is shadowing the field. Like they have the same name, so the line just assigns the parameter to itself. Nothing reaches the field." She said it slowly, testing it as she went, the way you'd step on ice. "So the object gets built, but the field stays null. Silently. No error, nothing."

Guneet stopped chewing. "So it looks correct and it does nothing?"

"Basically a perfect crime," Hannah said.

She reached past Marko for the keyboard, deleted the two lines, and typed this.name = name; and this.age = age; Marko started to ask what the word meant and then stopped himself, watching her run the test again. The output printed the names. All of them, in order, exactly as typed. Guneet applauded with pretzels dust on her hands.

"There's a keyword," Hannah said, mostly to fix it in her own memory. "This. It means the object's own field." She said it and immediately felt the sentence was too small for what it had just done, but there it was. She thought about her mother, who had wanted her to take the bookkeeping certificate because it was certain work, and about Ms. Francis, who had told her in the hallway that programming was mostly sitting alone with your own mistakes. Both of them, she suspected, were half right, though not the same halves. What she liked about the null output was that it had been honest in a way people rarely were: it had failed without pretending otherwise, and it had waited, without complaint, for her to notice.

Marko opened a new file and began writing a second class, Product, with the same bug in it on purpose, to see whether he could catch it himself now. Guneet found a deck of cards under the couch and started building a card house on the arm of the beanbag chair, narrating its structural flaws. Hannah saved the Student file twice, then a third time, and pulled the assignment sheet from her pocket to check what came next. There was a whole list: setters, a toString method, a test that checked for invalid ages. At the bottom, in small print, it said the placement test would include at least one question she could not prepare for.

She read that line again. Then she closed the sheet, tapped the desk twice, and said, "Okay, Marko. Hand over the keyboard."

He held onto it for a moment, considering, the cursor blinking on his deliberately broken Product class.

"One condition," he said. "You have to prognosticate first."

activity: graduating from high school
knowledge_domain: graduating from high school
fact: The square graduation cap is called a mortarboard because it resembles the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar.
story:
The cap kept sliding off Charles's head every time the wind came through the open door of Giordano's, and he finally took it off and set it on the table between the bread basket and his mother's water glass. Drew reached over and turned it in his hands like he was appraising a strange plate. "Why would they make it like this," Drew said. "A square board. It's the worst possible hat."

Charles had actually looked this up two weeks ago, after the fitting, when the tassel had hung down in front of his eye all through a rehearsal. "It's called a mortarboard," he said. "Because it looks like the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar." Drew turned it over again, unconvinced, and Brooklynn said that was the most useless piece of information anyone had ever brought to a dinner, though she said it while smiling, and then she put the cap on her own head at an angle, tassel swinging, and held up her phone for a picture.

The table was crowded, eleven of them, his parents and his aunt and Drew's mother and a rotating cast of classmates who had claimed the corner booth. Charles's father had ordered for everyone before anyone sat down, which was his way of celebrating, and the waiter kept arriving with plates nobody could match to a person. His father raised his glass and said a few things about Charles being the first in the family to start at a university in the fall, and his mother looked at Charles quickly, the way she always did when his father talked about it, because they both knew what the last six months had been like at the shop.

The shop. His father's hardware store had come close to insolvency that winter, and only a loan from his uncle had kept the doors open. Charles had heard the word insolvency first from his mother, on a Tuesday in January, said quietly on the back steps. He was fairly sure his father didn't know he knew. His father was mercurial in those months, expansive at dinner and silent in the car, and Charles had spent the spring being angry at him and then not being angry at him, the two states trading places depending on the day.

He had never quite figured out whether to say anything. Drew thought he should. Brooklynn thought he shouldn't, and she had written him a message about it, which he had read maybe ten times.

Brooklynn had texted: "I know you think you owe your dad some big conversation, but I don't think you owe anyone a performance of forgiveness. Either you forgive him or you don't. You don't have to announce it. Also I saw the numbers you were doing, for tuition, and you should let me see them again because I think you made an error in October." That was Brooklynn. She believed feelings were mostly private and math was mostly public, and she held both positions without apology.

Drew believed the opposite, mostly. He thought things unsaid turned into walls, that Charles's father probably lay awake wanting his son to exonerate him, or at least to say out loud that the store failing wasn't a moral failure, just a bad year with bad luck in it. "He's not a fraud," Drew had said on the drive over, one hand on the wheel of his mother's car. "He's a guy whose business almost died. There's a difference and you know it."

Charles had sat with both of them for most of the spring, and what he had arrived at was smaller than either of their positions and harder to say. He thought his father deserved something, and he thought he himself deserved not to have to perform it, and he could not fully reconcile those, and he suspected he never would, and he had decided somewhere in April that the honest position was to admit the two of them sat side by side like the two halves of that stupid square hat. When the waiter came with the tiramisu, his father stood up again for another toast, and Charles stood up too, before his father could start.

"I looked it up," Charles said, holding the mortarboard over his head with one hand. "This hat. It's called a mortarboard because it looks like the flat board bricklayers use to hold mortar. That's it. That's the whole reason." Everyone laughed, his aunt loudest, and his father looked at him with a cautious half-smile, waiting for the point. "So I wanted to say, I know about the store. Mom told me in January. And I don't need to make a speech about it either way. I just didn't want it to be the thing we never say at dinner." He put the cap back on, and the tassel swung into his eye, and Brooklynn lifted her phone and took the picture anyway.

activity: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
knowledge_domain: moving to a new town and leaving old friends behind
fact: A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back in student housing found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends.
story:
The boxes shifted in the trunk every time the car took a curve, and Andrew kept his hand pressed against the window as though steadying himself against the road. His father drove with the careful attention of a man who had rehearsed this trip, and the new town was still four hours away, which meant Andrew had until midnight and not a minute more to submit his residence preference to the university. First-year students chose online, ranked in order of arrival at the deposit page, and by seven that evening the remaining rooms would be gone. He had the portal open on his phone, a map of the building with two options left: a corner room on the third floor, larger, with a view of the quad, or a smaller room directly beside the main stairwell.

He called Kenneth first, because Kenneth had taken psychology second semester and would know if any of it mattered.

"Ask me the real question," Kenneth said, garrulous even over speakerphone, already halfway into a story about his cousin's dorm before Andrew could speak. "Is it the room or the people?"

"It's the people," Andrew said. "Obviously. You don't make friends because of where you live."

"You literally became friends with Maliyah because your lockers were next to each other. Freshman year. You complained about her stickers for a month and then you were inseparable."

Andrew said nothing. His father's eyes flicked toward the phone, then back to the road, the wipers clearing a fine mist that hadn't been falling when they left.

"We did a unit on this," Kenneth went on. "A 1950 study by Leon Festinger, Stanley Schachter and Kurt Back, in student housing. They found that people living closer together, or near shared stairways, were more likely to become friends."

"So it's a housing study from the fifties. People wrote letters back then."

"People still walked up stairways back then," Kenneth said. "Which is kind of the whole point."

Andrew hung up mildly annoyed and called Maliyah, who was quieter about it but no less certain. She had already chosen her own dorm for the fall, and she had chosen, she admitted, by the same logic Kenneth had recited, though she had arrived at it earlier, in her own way. Her older sister had gone to the same school and had watched a shy girl on her floor become the center of everything simply because her door faced the stairwell where everyone passed.

"You're treating it like it's fate versus chance," Maliyah said. "It's not. It's just probability. The stairwell room gives you more chances. The corner room gives you a nicer window."

"Maybe I don't want to be friends with whoever's loudest on the stairs."

"Then don't be. Nobody's forcing you. But you're deciding as if friendship is only about who you choose, and it's also about who you run into." She paused, and in the pause Andrew heard how much she was not saying, which was that she was one of the people he was leaving, and that she knew it. "That's the part you keep sublimating, by the way. You turn missing us into some big principle about authenticity."

"That's not what sublimate means."

"It's close enough. You turn it into a theory so you don't have to feel it."

He looked at the map on his screen. The corner room had a real appeal, and not only the window. It was set apart, and being set apart felt like a decision, like something he had reasoned his way toward rather than something that had happened to him. He had spent the summer telling himself that the move was an opportunity to be deliberate, to choose his friends carefully instead of drifting into them, and Kenneth's fifties study was unwelcome precisely because it suggested the drifting had never been aimless. Living near the stairwell, being a door people passed, these were not passive things. They were the mechanism, if he could use that word, by which a person met anyone at all.

But he was honest enough, watching the mile markers, to admit he couldn't be sure. Maybe he would take the stairwell room and resent the noise, or take it and meet nobody, or take the corner room and meet the best friend of his life at the far end of the hall. There was no controlling for it. Maliyah had used the word confounder once in statistics, a variable that tangles the effect you're studying with something else entirely, and he suspected his whole personality might be a confounder here. A person who wanted solitude could have the busiest doorway in the building and still eat alone.

It was eight minutes to seven when he made the choice, which was later than he meant it to be and earlier than it felt. He tapped the stairwell room, confirmed, and the page thanked him in gray sans-serif. His father, who had listened to both calls without a word, pulled into a gas station and cut the engine.

"The corner room had a better view," his father said.

"The stairwell has better odds," Andrew said, and watched his father consider this, weighing it the way he weighed everything, before nodding once and getting out to fill the tank. Andrew leaned his head against the cold window and texted Kenneth two words, stairwell room, and Kenneth sent back a thumbs-up and then, a moment later, a photograph of the two of them at graduation, neither of them looking at the camera, taken by Maliyah from three lockers down.

activity: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
knowledge_domain: how social, economic and environmental systems influence one another
fact: Adding lanes to a congested highway often fails to reduce traffic for long, because faster trips attract more driving until the new space fills; this effect is called induced demand.
story:
Aiden knelt in the dirt of the Miller Street community garden with a hose that leaked more water on his sneakers than on the tomato rows, and behind him, across the chain-link fence, cars sat bumper to bumper on Route 9, honking at nothing. He had come to weed because Mr. Chanthavong had promised him forty dollars and, more quietly, because his mother had said the apartment was too small for a boy home from his last summer before college. The garden occupied a wedge of land the city had almost sold twice, and its air smelled of hot asphalt, basil, and the faint rotten sweetness of last year's compost.

"They approved it," said Jaylynn, arriving through the gate with a bag of peaches and no explanation. "The council. Three to two. They're going to widen Route 9."

Aiden sat back on his heels. "Widen it how?"

"Two more lanes. They had the meeting last night. My dad went and yelled at a man in a polo shirt, which was the best thing that happened all week." Jaylynn dropped onto the overturned bucket Aiden used as a stool and offered him a peach. "They're going to take the fence line. Maybe ten feet of the garden."

Aiden looked at the fence. It was close enough that he could read the bumper stickers on the idling cars, and one of them, absurdly, said GROW LOCAL. Beyond the tomatoes, Ariane was filling jugs at the spigot for the plots tended by the older women who came on Thursdays in wide hats, and behind the whole garden the highway exhaled heat. He thought of the two perspectives he'd been carrying around all summer like coins in the same pocket: his father's, which held that congestion was a tax on everyone who worked for a living and that roads should be built until the tax disappeared, and Mr. Chanthavong's, which held that the garden was a small argument the neighborhood was making against the road, four dollars of tomatoes at a time.

"That's the plot with the ground cherries," he said. "Mrs. Okafor's. She'd lose the whole thing."

"They said traffic would move faster. Less time stuck, more money in people's pockets, less gas burned idling." Jaylynn bit into a peach with the commitment of someone who had rehearsed the argument at a dinner table and lost.

Aiden had heard that reasoning before, in his father's voice, and it had always sounded solid, the way a wall sounds solid until you push on one brick. He had spent a chunk of June reading through the transportation department's own reports for a civics paper, mostly to prove his father right, and had instead found a chart he still thought about in the shower. "Here's the thing," he said. "I read this. When they added lanes to the interstate back in the nineties, the trips got faster, so more people drove, until the new space filled up again. It has a name. Induced demand."

Jaylynn stopped chewing. "So the lanes don't work?"

"They work for a while. Then people who took the bus start driving, because the trip's faster, and people who drove at odd hours drive at rush hour, and it fills. That's what the data showed. The road eats whatever you feed it." He wiped peach juice on his jeans. "I wanted it to be wrong. My dad's whole commute, the route he's driven since I was six, I wanted the fix to be lanes."

Ariane came over with two jugs sloshing and stood listening with her head tilted, the way she did in seminar when someone was halfway to a point. "So if they take ten feet of the garden to build lanes that fill up again," she said slowly, "we lose ground cherries and gain nothing."

"That's the shape of it," Aiden said. "But I want to be honest. The reports cover that highway, not this one. And maybe the bus line out here is bad enough that the new drivers won't come from it. I don't know. I know the pattern, not this road."

Mr. Chanthavong emerged from the shed with a wheelbarrow and the expression of a man who had already heard the news through the open windows of the duplex next door. He did not aggrandize the loss; he said only, "Then we should say so where it counts. The vote on the easement is Tuesday. Three minutes at the microphone each." He looked at Aiden. "You read the reports. Bring the chart."

Aiden spent the evening in the garden instead of going home, printing the chart at the library and rehearsing at the compost bins while moths ran their small circuits around the solar lamp. Ariane helped him cut the numbers down to what a tired council member could absorb, and Jaylynn provided incisive commentary from the bucket, mostly consisting of "say that part louder" and "do not open with my dad's yelling."

On Tuesday the chamber smelled of floor wax and burnt coffee. Aiden's three minutes went fast; he heard his own voice go flat and careful, saying the words about faster trips and more driving and the name of the effect, and he watched the polo-shirt man lean toward a colleague and murmur. When he finished, a council member asked whether the pattern held on roads like Route 9, and Aiden said, truthfully, that he didn't know for certain, that the data was from elsewhere, and that it seemed worth finding out before the fence came down.

The easement vote was continued to September, pending a traffic study. In the parking lot afterward, Jaylynn whooped once and then stopped, because none of them knew what a study would say. Aiden drove home the long way, past the garden, where the tomatoes had gone dark and the fence still stood, and he slowed just enough to see, under the lamp, Mrs. Okafor already out with a flashlight, picking the ground cherries in case.

activity: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
knowledge_domain: to explain how greenhouse gases trap heat and read a graph of carbon dioxide over the last century
fact: The Keeling Curve zigzags every year because Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide as they grow in spring and summer, then release it as leaves die and decay in autumn and winter.
story:
Lea spread the printout on the picnic table, weighting its corners with two garden stones and a jar of screws nobody had ever returned to the garage. The graph looked like a saw blade laid on its side, a rising line torn into teeth, and she had been staring at it for ten minutes before Sandrine came through the back gate carrying her own copy, folded carelessly into her back pocket.

"Yours has the wiggles too," Lea said. She kept her voice even, though her first thought, all morning, had been that the machine in Hawaii was broken. "I figured mine was a bad print."

Sandrine unfolded her page against the table and flattened it with her palm. "Same wiggles. Every year, up and down, up and down, and the whole thing still climbing." She tapped the sawteeth with one finger. "Gaelle says it's not noise. She says it's the trees."

"The trees."

"Think about what trees do." Sandrine had that way of pausing after a question, letting it sit until the other person had to answer it. She sat on the bench, pushed her hair off her forehead, and waited.

Lea looked past her at the backyard, at the maple dropping its first brown leaves onto the trampoline, at the flowerbeds gone to stalks. Something moved in her head slowly, like a drawer sliding open. Plants take in carbon dioxide. They take it in when they grow, in spring and summer, and then autumn comes, and the leaves die and fall and decay, and it goes back out. Half the world's land and most of its seasons are north of the equator, the Northern Hemisphere doing all that breathing at once. The graph was not broken. The graph was the planet breathing.

"That's why it drops every summer," she said. "Not drops forever. Drops a little. The plants are pulling it in, all of them at once, and then they let it go again in the fall and winter, and it climbs back, and then some. So the teeth." She heard how fast she was talking and slowed down. "So the teeth."

Sandrine smiled without saying anything, which was its own kind of confirmation.

They worked through the afternoon. Lea had agreed, somewhat against her will, to explain the whole thing to her father tonight, because he had spent a decade insisting that climate data was manufactured to frighten people, and Ms. Crowchild, their old biology teacher, had told Lea at graduation that the only argument worth having was the one you could make to someone who loved you. Lea was not sure she wanted that argument. She practiced anyway, walking the yard with the printout, saying it aloud to the maple.

"Sunlight comes through, the earth warms, the earth radiates heat back out, and gases like carbon dioxide let the light in but absorb the outgoing heat, so more of it stays near the surface. More gas, more heat kept." She said it to the fence, to the clothesline, to a querulous squirrel that scolded her from the maple's lowest branch and refused to be soothed. Each time she got a little smoother, and a little more suspicious of her own smoothness, because smoothness was what she distrusted in people who argued at dinner tables.

At dusk her father came out with two glasses of iced tea and sat where Sandrine had been. Lea pushed the graph across to him. He put on his glasses, which she took as a good sign, and studied it in silence for longer than she expected.

"The little squiggles," he said finally. "What are those, instrument error?"

Something in her relaxed, because it was the same mistake she had made, and she knew the road out of it. "That's what I thought. But they're real. They happen every single year, the same size, the same rhythm." She pointed at one tooth, then the next. "Northern Hemisphere plants take in carbon dioxide when they grow, in spring and summer. That's the dip. Then the leaves die and decay in autumn and winter and it gets released again. That's the rise back. The whole hemisphere breathing in and out, once a year."

He leaned closer. "Every year."

"Every year. And underneath the breathing, it's climbing." She did not say more than that. She had planned a speech about evidence and honesty and the difference between skepticism and refusal, had rehearsed sentences that would have adjudicated the whole dispute in her favor, and she let them go. She could not prove to him tonight what was true; she could only show him what she had seen. Whether the breathing planet,锯ing its slow way upward across the page, would reach him where words had not, she genuinely did not know.

He traced the line with one fingertip, following a tooth down and up, then the next tooth, and said, "Read me the top number again."

activity: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
knowledge_domain: to lead a holiday meal ceremony from start to finish for the whole family
fact: During Ramadan, many Muslims break each day's fast at the sunset meal, iftar, by first eating a date, following the practice of the Prophet Muhammad.
story:
The sun hung a knuckle's width above the rooftops when Lucas realized he had left the dates in his father's car, three blocks from the mosque basement where forty relatives and neighbours were already settling into folding chairs. His grandmother had handed him the box that morning with a gravity he had tried not to aggrandize, since it was only fruit, after all, only a box of dates, though everyone in the room knew it was not only anything.

"You're pacing," said Gregoire, who had come to help carry chairs even though he wasn't fasting and didn't have to be there at all. "You're doing the hallway thing."

"I'm not doing a hallway thing. I'm timing the sun."

The plan had been his idea, proposed at the kitchen table two weeks ago with a confidence that now embarrassed him. This year, he had said, he would run the iftar from start to finish: the table, the water, the food, the moment itself. His father would sit among the guests instead of standing at the door. His mother had looked at him for a long second and then said only, "Then you'll need to be exact," and he had understood that exactness was the whole assignment.

At the folding table near the window, Baby was arranging glasses of water in rows and making them worse, or so it seemed, until Lucas saw that she was grouping them by family so that no one would have to reach across anyone. She had done that without being asked. He had spent the week memorizing the order of things, the small liturgy of the meal, and had barely thought about the people doing the eating. "The dates matter most," he told her, crouching beside the table. "That's how everyone breaks the fast. One date first, at sunset. It's what the Prophet Muhammad did, so we do it too."

"Why a date and not, like, an apple?"

"I don't know why. That part nobody ever told me. I just know it comes first, before anything, before even the water." He heard his own voice and worried it sounded like a lecture, though Baby only nodded and moved a glass two inches to the left.

He ran the hallway again, out the side door and down the steps, and there was his father already coming toward him with the box held against his chest like something rescued from a fire. They stopped a metre apart in the late light. His father did not say that Lucas had forgotten; there had been a quiet detente between them since the kitchen-table proposal, a truce in which his father did not hover and Lucas did not ask for hovering, and they both honoured it now by speaking only of the sky. "Nine minutes," his father said, tilting his chin at the orange rim on the rooftops. "Maybe less." Then, just as Lucas turned to go, "Your grandmother counted on you."

In the basement Lucas set the box at the head of the table, opened it, and began laying dates along the edge of each plate, one per person, his hands steadier than he expected. Ms. Katz, who taught history at the school and lived next door to the mosque and had been invited by his mother for reasons that were probably tangential to religion and probably not, leaned over the table and asked what the fruit was for. He explained again, the same short version: the fast breaks at sunset, at the meal called iftar, and it begins with a date, because that was the practice of the Prophet Muhammad. "So it's a tradition and a clock at the same time," she said, and that was more accurate than anything he had managed to say all week.

When the light through the high windows went grey and then blue, his grandmother, seated nearest the window with her hands folded, said without opening her eyes, "Now." Lucas lifted the first date and put it into her open hand, and around the table the small sounds began, paper peeling, water poured, chairs shifting closer, forty people eating one date each in the moment the sun left the sky. He stood at the head of it all, not eating yet, watching to make sure nobody was missed, and Gregoire caught his eye from across the room and raised a glass of water like a toast.

There would be a next year, and he would probably forget something next year too. His father had taken a chair among the guests, as promised, and was looking up at him, waiting, a date held unpeeled in his fingers. Lucas picked one up for himself, sat down, and said, "So. Bismillah."

activity: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
knowledge_domain: to write a research paper with an argument, footnotes and a bibliography in a standard citation style
fact: A research paper's thesis must be arguable, a claim a reasonable person could dispute, rather than a fact everyone already accepts.
story:
The draft came back on a Thursday, folded into Ashton's backpack with a sticky note in Ms. Pham's small, upright handwriting: "A thesis has to be arguable. Come see me." He read it three times on the bus, and by the time he got to his grandfather's house, where he spent every Thursday afternoon while his mother worked the late shift, he had decided the note was a kind of insult. His thesis, on the second page of the draft, said that the Marshall Plan rebuilt Western Europe after the war. Who could argue with that? It was in the textbook. It was in three of his sources.

His grandfather was at the kitchen table with the radio on low, doing the crossword in pen, which he claimed was a matter of principle. Ashton dropped his backpack on the chair opposite and told him the whole thing, how Ms. Pham had written "arguable?" in the margin next to his thesis, twice, the second time underlined.

"Is she wrong?" his grandfather asked, not looking up.

"No. That's the worst part." Ashton pulled out the draft and flattened it on the table. "But I don't get what she wants. I found good sources. I have footnotes. I did the bibliography in the style she gave us, the whole thing, alphabetical, hanging indents, everything."

His grandfather filled in a word, seven letters, and set the pen down. "So a thesis is an argument," he said, half to himself. "And a fact is just a fact."

"Right, but the Marshall Plan is important. Isn't that enough?"

"Important and arguable aren't the same thing," his grandfather said. "Nobody disputes the sun came up this morning. Doesn't make for much of a conversation."

Ashton sat with that. He texted Sydney, who was in the same class and had gotten her draft back with only a checkmark, which he still resented. She wrote back, "mine is 'the Marshall Plan served American strategic interests more than European ones.' she circled it and wrote YES." He read it twice. Sydney's claim could be disagreed with. Somebody reasonable, somebody who had read the same documents, could say no, actually, it was humanitarian. Nobody could reasonably say the Marshall Plan didn't happen.

"So the whole paper is a fight," he said slowly. "Like, a polite fight, on paper, with footnotes."

"Every good one I ever read," his grandfather said. He got up to put the kettle on, which he did whenever a conversation had gone on longer than five minutes, as if thinking required tea. "You know my brother was what they called a dissident, back home. He wrote things the government didn't like. The point wasn't that he was right about everything. The point was that somebody wanted him not to say it. That's how you knew it was worth saying."

Ashton had heard about the great-uncle in fragments over the years, letters that went missing, a period of years no one would account for. He'd always thought of it as family history, tangential to his own life, the kind of thing that belonged to other people's paper topics. Now it occurred to him that his grandfather had just handed him something: an entire paper could be about what the Marshall Plan was for, whom it served, what it cost and who paid. He took out a fresh sheet of paper and started writing questions instead of statements. Was the Plan charity or strategy? Could it be both at once, and did the answer change depending on which documents you trusted?

"Look at you," his grandfather said, setting down two mugs.

"I don't have a thesis yet," Ashton warned him. "I have, like, six, and they fight each other."

"Then pick the fight you actually believe." His grandfather returned to the crossword, then paused. "Though I'll tell you, the older I get, the less I trust anybody who's certain. Even myself."

That was the part Ashton kept chewing on through dinner and the drive home. Ms. Pham wanted a claim a reasonable person could dispute, but she also kept saying, in class, that the evidence had to lead where it led. What if the sources pulled both directions? He had one historian calling the Plan economic containment, another calling it reconstruction, a third saying the distinction was invented after the fact. He texted Jared, who knew everything about everything, and Jared wrote back a long thing about hedge words, and Ashton typed, then deleted, then typed: "but if I hedge everything, what am I even arguing?"

Friday morning he found Ms. Pham before first period, draft in hand. He'd circled the paragraph where his old thesis used to be and written above it, "The Marshall Plan's economic terms made European recovery serve American markets more than European independence." He handed it over and waited while she read.

"Better," she said. "Somebody could dispute that."

"Somebody in my sources already disputes it," Ashton said. "One guy says the opposite, basically, and I sort of believe both of them a little."

Ms. Pham smiled and handed the draft back. "That's usually where the interesting papers live." Then she said, "By the way, Sydney came to me yesterday worried her thesis was too strong. I told her to consider the counterargument more. She's now rewriting everything."

Ashton stood there a moment, holding his paper.

"So she got the YES circled and now she has to redo it?"

"Welcome to research," Ms. Pham said, and walked into her classroom.

activity: taking a first driving lesson
knowledge_domain: taking a first driving lesson
fact: In a car with anti-lock brakes, a driver in an emergency should press the brake firmly and hold it rather than pump it, and can still steer.
story:
Tyson sat on the front step with the owner's manual open across his knees, though he was really watching the street for Ms. Kamau's car. His grandfather had come by at breakfast, before his shift at the depot, and had leaned in the doorway with his coffee while Tyson signed the permission forms.

"Pump the brakes if you ever have to stop fast," his grandfather had said. "That's what my father taught me. Squeeze and let go, squeeze and let go. That's how you keep her from skidding." He had said it the way he said most things, like a fact about the weather, and Tyson had nodded, the way he always nodded, and now he wasn't sure. The road test was tomorrow at nine, and there was only this one lesson between him and it.

Ms. Kamau arrived in a small hatchback with a sign on the roof and a second brake pedal bolted beside hers. "Radio off, phone in the glovebox," she said, pulling the keys from her pocket. "You've read the handbook?" Tyson held up the manual. "Good. Then contextualize that for me. Where are we, and where are we going?"

"Home to the school parking lot, then the hill streets, then home," he said. "About forty minutes."

"Ninety minutes," she said. "You're not just learning routes today. You're learning what the car does when you're frightened." She seemed to expect him to find that useful rather than alarming, so he decided to try.

The parking lot first: three-point turns, smooth stops, her clipboard scratching in the quiet. Then the hill streets, where an ancient Buick sat parked at an angle so severe it looked abandoned, and Ms. Kamau said, "That's an antiquated idea of parking, Tyson. Hills get chocks now, or a good wheel turn. Steer past it." He steered past it, and she let a silence open up in which he could hear his own breathing slow.

His phone buzzed once in the glovebox around then, and later, at a red light, she allowed him thirty seconds to check it. Gabriela: u have ur lesson today right?? blaine says the tester on Fridays is a nightmare, fails everyone on hills. He typed back, i'm on the lesson now, and put it away, but the deadline tightened around him like a strap. One lesson. One tester, possibly a nightmare.

They were coming down Alder, a long residential slope with parked cars close on both sides, when a cat came off a porch and ran into the road. Not far. Ten feet ahead, maybe less. His grandfather's voice arrived instantly, squeeze and let go, and Tyson's foot actually began to obey it, press, release, press, and the car was not slowing the way it needed to, and the wheel felt loose and wrong in his hands, and then something older than either of them took over. He pressed the brake as hard as he could and held it. The pedal buzzed and shuddered under his foot like something alive, and for half a second he thought he'd broken the car, but the hatchback kept tracking straight, still answering the wheel, and he steered, gently, and the car turned while it stopped, and the cat vanished under a hedge with its tail up.

He pulled over, hands still on the wheel, and the reverie he fell into was short and vivid: his grandfather at nineteen, on some ice-covered road in a car with none of this, pumping because pumping was what kept you alive then. It wasn't stupid advice. It was just advice from a different machine.

"The buzzing," Tyson said. His voice came out steadier than he expected. "That's the anti-lock brakes."

"That's the anti-lock brakes," Ms. Kamau agreed. "You pressed and held, and you steered while it stopped." She wrote nothing on her clipboard, which somehow felt like more than writing something. "Your grandfather taught you to pump?"

"Yeah. This morning." He looked at the pedal as if it might speak. "I started to. Out there. It didn't work, and then I just held it down."

"There are two kinds of knowing in you now," she said. "The one that came first, and the one that just happened. Tomorrow, under pressure, you'll find out which one is louder. That's not a criticism. That's just what pressure is."

He drove home with the radio still off, taking the hills slowly, and when they pulled into his driveway his grandfather was there, home early, washing his truck in the driveway with a rag that had seen better decades. He came over and rapped a knuckle on the hatchback's roof.

"How'd he do?"

Tyson got out and stood between the two of them, the old teacher and the new one, with his hands still remembering the buzz.

"A cat ran out on Alder," Tyson said. "I held the brake down and steered around it. The pedal buzzed, and it just stopped." His grandfather looked at him for a long moment, rag twisting in his fist. "Held it, huh," his grandfather said. "Well. Show me where it says that in the book."

activity: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
knowledge_domain: to build a class in Java with private fields and getter methods and test it
fact: A getter that returns a reference to a private mutable object, such as a list, lets outside code change it, so programmers often return a copy instead.
story:
The computer lab at Camp Wawetkin smelled of pine sap and overheated keyboards, and Luca had claimed the terminal by the window because it was the only one where the fan didn't sound like a dying lawnmower. Their counselor, Mr. Almeida, had given them a project: build a class in Java, private fields, getter methods, and a test to prove it all worked. Luca had decided to write a class called CabinRoster, because the real cabin roster was taped to the door of Cabin 4 and read like a hostage negotiation. If the roster lived in code, he reasoned, it couldn't be argued with. It could be an autocrat, benevolent but absolute, and Luca liked the sound of that.

He typed fast for the first twenty minutes, then hit the wall that every wall at camp was made of: Kashton, who leaned across the aisle with the confidence of someone about to be extremely wrong. "You can't peek at my test scores, so your class shouldn't peek at my fields," Kashton said. "That's basically the whole point of private."

"I know that," Luca said. "That's why I wrote getScores. It returns the list. Everything is fine."

Everything was not fine. Luca discovered this at 11:40, when he ran his test and watched the printed roster come out empty, blank, gutted, like the lake after the drought two summers ago. He had put eleven campers in that list. Now there were zero, and the program chirped its cheerful "BUILD SUCCESSFUL" at him as if it had done him a favor.

He leaned back. "Kashton. Did you touch my roster?"

Kashton held up his hands, palms out, the universal gesture of a boy standing near a crime scene. "I called the getter. That's it. I just wanted to see who was in your cabin so I could check if Maggie was on it."

"She's in Cabin 6, and you know that, and also that's not the point." Luca scrolled through Kashton's class, the one called PrankEngine, because of course it was called PrankEngine. There it was: a single line that called getRoster and then called clear on whatever came back. Kashton swore he'd only meant to clear his own list, a list of targets for a water balloon campaign that was, by his own admission, endemic to Cabin 5, a tradition so widespread the counselors had given up policing it.

Luca stared at the line. His field was private. His getter was public. Somehow the private list had been emptied anyway, and the more he looked, the more it seemed that the getter hadn't handed over a locked box; it had handed over the box itself, list and all, with the key still in it. He said as much out loud, slowly, testing it. "It's like I gave you my diary and said don't write in it, and then you wrote in it."

"I would never write in your diary," Kashton said. "Your diary is boring. Your roster, however, was an intelligence asset."

Mr. Almeida drifted past their row the way he did, hands behind his back, radiating the calm of a man who had spent June recovering from knee surgery and was still, in his words, convalescing from the experience of teaching middle school. He looked at Luca's screen for exactly four seconds. "Interesting," he said, and walked on, which was the most infuriating thing a counselor could possibly do.

Luca spent lunch turning it over while Maggie, who had wandered over from the Java section of the waterfront table, stole his pretzels and offered commentary. "So the fix is what, make the list private-er? Is there private-plus-plus?"

"There's no private-plus-plus," Luca said. "I checked. Twice." He turned his napkin over and sketched it: the getter didn't have to return the actual list. It could return a copy, a duplicate made fresh every time someone asked. Then outside code could clear the copy until the heat death of the universe and the real roster would sit untouched behind the private wall, smug and intact. It felt almost like cheating, like he was lying about what he was handing over. But it also felt like the only version of the word private that actually meant something. Two ideas he'd been holding separately, that sharing was polite and that some things were yours, clicked together into something with an actual edge to it: you could share the shape of a thing without handing over the thing itself.

After rest hour he rewrote the getter, ran Kashton's PrankEngine against it, and watched the copy get emptied while the printed roster still showed all eleven campers, serene as a row of ducks. He was still not entirely sure it was the right answer rather than just a working one. What if someone wanted to add a camper from outside the class? Would they have to call a method every time, forever? The whole design suddenly felt like a set of doors, and he wasn't sure he'd chosen the right number of locks.

Kashton leaned over, read the output, and groaned. "So my prank engine is useless against you now."

"Your prank engine was always useless," Maggie said. "It's held together by comments and hope."

Luca saved the file, then, on impulse, added a twelfth camper to the roster and labeled it KASHTON, WATER BALLOON TARGET, PRIMARY. He printed the roster to the shared lab printer, walked it back to Kashton's terminal, and laid it down beside the keyboard.

"Intelligence asset," Kashton said, picking it up, "for the other side."

activity: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
knowledge_domain: to give honest feedback to a teammate in a way that is specific and kind
fact: Researcher Amy Edmondson described 'psychological safety' in 1999 as a team's shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks, such as admitting a mistake.
story:
The party had been Callen's idea, mostly, a combined birthday thing for the two of them since their dates fell three days apart, and now it was ten o'clock and the group project was due at midnight and the laptop sat open on the kitchen counter between a bowl of chips and somebody's abandoned cup of punch.

"Okay, watch it," Callen said. "Final cut. Don't talk during my favorite part."

Brooklyn stood beside Matteo while the video played, and she felt the same foreboding she'd felt every time she'd watched it this week, a tightening behind her ribs that had nothing to do with the party noise or the deadline. The documentary was good. Callen had shot most of it, edited all of it, stayed up two nights running on vending machine coffee, and it was good, except for the middle section, where the interview with the crossing guard cut off mid-sentence and jumped to footage of the parking lot, and the on-screen caption misspelled the woman's name.

"That's the one," Callen said when it ended, arms folded, grinning. "That's the best thing I've ever made."

Matteo said, "It's really good," and reached for the chips.

He had seen the glitch. Brooklyn knew he had, because they'd stood together at lunch on Thursday and he'd pointed at the screen with his straw and then lowered it without saying anything. Nobody in the group had said anything. For two weeks they had all watched the error sit there like a stain on a rug, and for two weeks the only feedback anyone gave Callen was "great" and "love it," and Callen beamed a little more each time, and Brooklyn had beamed too, and hated herself for it.

"Ten-fifteen," Matteo said, checking his phone. "If we're uploading, we should upload."

"You can't fix anything in forty-five minutes," Brooklyn said.

Callen turned. "Fix what?"

There it was. Her mother called her canny, said she always knew which way the wind was blowing before anyone else felt it, and Brooklyn had always taken it as praise until recently, when she'd started noticing that knowing and saying were different muscles entirely.

"The crossing guard section," she said. "The clip ends mid-sentence. It cuts off when she's talking about her grandkids, and then it jumps. And the caption says her name is Darlene Marsh, but she told us Darla Marsh. I wrote it down."

Callen's face did something complicated. "It's ninety seconds out of eleven minutes."

"I know."

"Eleven minutes nobody else spent three nights on."

Brooklyn looked at Matteo, who had become extremely interested in the chip bowl. Somewhere in the living room somebody put on music, and the thudding bass made the counter hum. She thought about the article Mr. Brown had left on his desk last week, photocopied, dog-eared, that she'd read while waiting to ask about a deadline extension. She'd read it twice, actually, then a third time on her phone in bed.

"Can I tell you a thing I read?" she said. "It's not a burn. It's a thing."

Callen leaned against the fridge, arms still folded, which Brooklyn chose not to interpret as a door closing.

"There's this researcher, Amy Edmondson. In 1999 she wrote about this thing she called psychological safety. It's a team's shared belief that it's safe to take interpersonal risks, like admitting a mistake."

"So?"

"So think about who's been safe in our group. You weren't. If you'd shown us a rough cut a week ago and said, does anything feel off, we'd have had time. But you didn't, because you thought you had to hand us something perfect. And we weren't either, because Matteo saw the jump cut on Thursday and said nothing, and I saw the name thing and said nothing, because it was easier to let you walk into midnight with a broken video than to risk being the person who ruined the mood." She took a breath. "That's not a team. That's an audience."

The kitchen was quiet except for the bass. Matteo said, quietly, "I did see it. Thursday. I'm sorry, Cal."

Callen stared at the paused frame on the screen, the parking lot, empty and gray. "The Marsh part's my favorite section," he said. "That's why I kept it even though the ending was messy. I couldn't cut her grandkids story and I couldn't fix it either."

"Can you fix it in forty minutes?"

"Maybe the caption. The jump cut, no. Not properly." He rubbed his eyes. "The clip's salvageable if I end it earlier, on her sentence about the rain, but it breaks the flow into the parking lot."

"Then it breaks the flow," Brooklyn said. "The deadline's real. Fix the name, trim the cut, and Tuesday we ask Mr. Brown for feedback before it's final. Like, a real rough cut. Where we say true things."
