"And people say true things back," Matteo said.

"And it's awful," Callen said, "and we do it anyway." He pulled the laptop toward him and started typing, fast, the way he did when he'd stopped arguing with himself. "Brooklyn, sit there and read me the name off your notes, you're the one who wrote it down, apparently, like a person with integrity."

She sat on the counter beside the chips and unfolded the crumpled page from her back pocket. "Darla Marsh. D-a-r-l-a."

Ten minutes to midnight they hit upload, the three of them crowded around the screen, and the progress bar crawled while Callen narrated every percentage like a sports announcer. The file landed at 11:58, and Matteo toasted them with punch, and Callen said, "Tuesday, rough cuts, and you both have to tell me one real problem with mine, minimum, or I'm not showing it."

"One minimum," Brooklyn agreed. "Possibly two."

"Bold of you to codify it," Callen said. "Fine. Two."

He closed the laptop and put his hand flat on it, like settling something. "Also, happy birthday, by the way. We never did the cake."

"Get the cake," Matteo said, already heading for the fridge.

activity: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
knowledge_domain: how unions, collective bargaining and labour laws shape wages, hours and working conditions
fact: The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 10.0 percent of wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, down from 20.1 percent in 1983.
story:
Marcus set his phone face-down on the dinner table before his grandfather arrived, which he told himself was courtesy, though really it was nerves. Ms. Farah had assigned an interview with a family member about their working life, due Monday, and Marcus had put it off until the last possible Sunday. His grandfather had spent thirty-one years at a stamping plant across the river, and Marcus remembered, or thought he remembered, a house full of union talk, everyone in it, everyone he knew of that generation belonging to something. He had even told Evie in the cafeteria that basically all workers back then carried a union card, and she had nodded and written it down, which was the trouble with saying things confidently.

"So you want the whole tour," his grandfather said, after the plates were served. "The plant, the layoffs, the strike of '85. I can amortize a story across three visits if you want the full payoff." Marcus laughed and said one dinner would do, and his mother made a noise that meant he should pass the potatoes first. He slid the dish, clicked his pen, and asked the first real question: what did the union actually change?

"Everything and nothing," his grandfather said, which was not a usable quote. Marcus pressed. "The wage. You got a rate, and it was printed, and nobody's cousin got hired in above you because he played golf with the supervisor. Hours, too. Overtime after forty, time and a half, in the contract. Safety gloves that actually existed." He talked about grievances, about a shop steward named Rudy who walked new hires through their rights the first day, and Marcus wrote fast, his handwriting collapsing into a kind of somnolence, so tired his letters drooped on the page. When the meal ended, half the story was still untold, so his grandfather took a napkin and, in a slow draftsman's hand, wrote him a note to read later, folded it twice, and pushed it across the tablecloth.

Marcus unfolded it while his mother cleared dishes. "You said in the cafeteria that everyone was in a union in my day," the note read, which startled him, because he had not known his grandfather was in that cafeteria, and later, texting Evie, he would learn she had mentioned it at the community dinner where her church group served the old men coffee. "Let me give you the actual numbers, because you strike me as a kid who likes those. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 10.0 percent of wage and salary workers were union members in 2025, down from 20.1 percent in 1983. So not everyone. Not even close, now. I was one of the ten percent. You will likely live your whole working life without being one." Below that he had drawn, for no reason Marcus could find, a small square with a diagonal through it.

"Did you know it dropped that much?" Marcus asked, holding up the napkin. His grandfather shrugged, sipped his coffee. "I watched it happen and couldn't have told you the figures. You'll have the figures and watch it happen anyway. That's a strange trade."

Later, upstairs, Marcus opened a message thread with John, who stocked shelves with him at the supermarket, and typed: my grandpa says only 10.0 percent of workers are union members now, it was 20.1 percent in 1983. John's reply came fast: so basically extinct. but check this, they cut Derek's hours to 19 a week last month so they don't have to give him benefits. nineteen. like exactly under some line. Marcus sat with that. He had been angry about his own schedule, how it slid around like weather, eleven hours one week, twenty-two the next, never enough to plan around and never enough to matter. He typed: what if we all asked together. John replied with a single word, sure, then a second message, though, and then nothing for a while, and Marcus understood the though. It was the sound of a thing that had been possible once and now had to be imagined back into existence, one stockroom at a time, with no steward named Rudy to walk them through it.

He did not finish the interview questions. Instead he wrote his grandfather a reply on notebook paper, since the man had no phone he would answer: I don't know if we can get back what you had, or if we'd even want all of it. But I found out tonight that we have less of it than I thought, and I had the numbers wrong, and so did you, kind of. He folded it into his pocket to hand over at breakfast.

Downstairs, the kitchen still smelled of coffee, and his mother asked if he'd gotten what he needed for the assignment. Marcus looked at the napkin, at the square with its diagonal line, and turned it over. On the back, smaller, his grandfather had added one more line: that square is the union's old stamp, the local's mark. I can still draw it with my eyes closed.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: All 50 US states and Washington, DC allow minors to consent to testing and treatment for sexually transmitted infections without a parent's permission, though some states set a minimum age.
story:
James had volunteered for the peer health track at Camp Wren because the application asked what he was afraid of, and he had written, after a long pause, "talking out loud about things that matter." Now, on the second Wednesday of July, he sat in the infirmary porch with a laminated script in his lap, learning to say words he had previously only encountered in the privacy of a search history. Mr. Goh, the camp nurse, had given him three modules: consent, contraception, and how to get tested for infections at a clinic. James was to present them to the younger campers on Friday.

"You're rushing it," Zainab said, watching him rehearse. She had appointed herself his audience on the condition that he never make eye contact with her during the word condom. "You say consent like a password. Like if you say it fast enough, no one will notice."

"That's the idea," James said, and started again. He slowed down. Consent, he explained to an imaginary circle of fifteen-year-olds, was ongoing, specific, and revocable; a yes to one thing was not a yes to everything, and a person who had been drinking could not meaningfully accede to anything. Zainab made him repeat the last part until it stopped sounding like a recitation of criminal law and started sounding like something he believed.

The contraception module went better, or at least more concretely. Mr. Goh had supplied a shoebox of demonstration items and a phlegmatic manner that made even the female condom seem about as scandalous as a wrist brace. James learned failure rates, and the difference between methods that protect against pregnancy and methods that also protect against infection. What he could not learn, and knew he could not, was how to say any of it to a room of people who would rather be at the lake.

It was Laila who broke the modules open. On Thursday evening she found him at the picnic table behind the dining hall and stood there twisting the strap of her water bottle until he closed his binder. "That clinic thing you're teaching," she said. "The one in town. Do they make a parent sign the form? Because my mother reads our mail." She said it flatly, the way you hand someone something heavy so they will take it quickly. James realized he did not know. He said he'd find out by morning.

He found Mr. Goh in the infirmary at seven, folding towels, and asked. The nurse was brief, not lecturing. "All fifty states and DC, minors can consent to testing and treatment for STIs on their own. No parent signature." James asked if that included Laila. "Some states set a minimum age," Mr. Goh said, "but she's past it. She can walk in and ask for a test herself." James wrote none of it down, because he understood that the moment he needed the words, they would have to sound like his own. He walked to the lake and said the whole fact out loud to the water until it sat in his mouth naturally, and even then he knew there was a gap between reciting a law and standing beside someone while she used it.

On Friday he presented to nineteen campers, and it went the way Zainab had predicted: badly for ten minutes, then suddenly not badly at all. A boy in the back asked whether the clinic put anything in the mail, and James heard himself answer with the law, plainly, without rushing, and saw the boy's shoulders come down an inch. Laila was not in the audience. She had taken the camp van into town that morning, alone, with a slip of paper Mr. Goh had drawn her a map on. Zainab caught James's eye across the circle and nodded once, and James felt the strange arithmetic of it, that his fear of speaking had cost him a year of silence and had been converted, in a single week, into something a stranger could breathe easier for.

The cost surfaced an hour later. Laila came back with a bandage on her arm and a leaflet folded into eighths, sat down next to him, and said nothing for a while. Then she said, "Negative. But you know what the nurse asked me? Whether my counselor had explained my options before I came in." James looked at her. "I said I learned it from a peer educator," she said. "She said, which one, we train half the county." And then, before he could decide what that meant, a girl from the youngest cabin tapped him on the shoulder and asked, very quietly, whether the part about consent was still true if the other person was your boyfriend.

activity: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
knowledge_domain: to explain consent, contraception and how to get tested for infections at a clinic
fact: Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way for a person to know whether they have one.
story:
The bathroom outside the gym smelled like disinfectant and wet paper towels, and John had chosen it because nobody used it after fifth period. He set his note cards on the edge of the sink, eight of them, and looked at himself in the mirror. Mr. Banerjee had asked him to run the health workshop for the sophomore advisory, and Mr. Banerjee had said it in the flat voice that did not portend a negotiation, so here John was, rehearsing to a paper towel dispenser.

"Consent has to be freely given," he said to the mirror. "It can be withdrawn at any time. If someone's been drinking, they can't meaningfully agree."

The stall door behind him opened. Danny came out, zipping his jacket, and stopped at the next sink. "You're talking to yourself."

"I'm practicing. Banerjee volunteered me."

"For what?"

John held up the cards. "Peer health thing. Consent, contraception, where to get tested. I present tomorrow."

Danny washed his hands slowly, like the water was a decision he was still making. He had been truculent all through junior year, quick with a shrug and a worse remark, and John mostly worked around him the way you worked around weather. Now Danny was quiet in a way that didn't fit him.

"What's the testing part," Danny said. "Like, how does that even work."

"There's a clinic on Marsh Street. Free, and they don't call your parents. You can walk in." John flipped to the card on contraception and back. "They do urine tests for the main stuff."

Danny turned the tap off. He didn't reach for the towels. "Say you feel fine, though," he said, watching John in the mirror instead of facing him. "Like, nothing hurts, nothing's weird. Then why bother going at all."

"That's the thing," John said. He'd read the clinic pamphlet four times the night before, partly because the workshop counted for a grade and partly because the sentence had stuck in his head like something he was supposed to say out loud to somebody. "Chlamydia and gonorrhea often cause no symptoms, so testing is the only reliable way to know whether you have one." He heard how it sounded, flat and pamphlet-like, and tried it again slower. "Feeling fine doesn't prove anything. That's the whole reason the clinic exists the way it does."

Danny wiped his hands on his jeans. Outside, a whistle went off in the gym, twice, the sound muffled through the cinderblock. Danny looked at the door like it might open on its own.

"When's your thing," Danny said. "Tomorrow?"

"Sixth period."

Danny took out his phone, unlocked it, held it low against his hip so John almost couldn't see. Then he turned it around. On the screen was a confirmation email from the Marsh Street clinic, an appointment slot tomorrow at 3:40, under a first name and last initial only. The date was from three weeks ago.

"You already went," John said.

"It was fine. They were nice. They just, whatever, they asked questions." Danny pocketed the phone. His ears had gone red, which John had never seen happen to him, not even the time the coach benched him for a whole half. "The thing is, that pamphlet you read. That sentence about symptoms. That was me who put it in."

"What?"

"Banerjee asked if anyone had questions to submit for the peer workshop, anonymous, drop box in his room. I wrote that question. About feeling fine." Danny turned the tap back on and let it run without putting his hands under it. "Because I felt fine, and I almost didn't go. And then I went anyway because a girl I know said the same thing happened to her and she only found out from a test."

The water ran. John put his cards down on the sink, squared them against the porcelain, and picked them up again. Somewhere in his head the workshop was rearranging itself, the rehearsed order dissolving into something he couldn't rehearse, something that would have to be a conversation instead of a presentation. He didn't know yet how you led a room of sophomores into that kind of conversation. He knew he'd been treating the whole thing as a heuristic, a card for consent and a card for clinics, a checklist that would run itself, and it wasn't a checklist.

"Can you sit in tomorrow," John said. "Not, like, present. Just be there."

Danny finally shut the tap off. "You'd point me out in front of everyone."

"I wouldn't." John picked up his backpack by one strap. "I just think it lands different when it's not coming from a pamphlet."

Danny looked at him for a second, then at the mirror, then at the cards in John's hand.

"I'll be in the back," he said, and pushed the door open with his shoulder.

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: A guitar in standard tuning has its six strings tuned, from lowest to highest, to E, A, D, G, B and E.
story:
The guitar had belonged to Aaron's grandfather, and it arrived at school on a Tuesday in a cardboard case that smelled of WD-40 and old wool. Mr. Novák had agreed to keep it in the band room storage closet between the timpani and the shelf of marching-band hats, mostly, Aaron suspected, because the alternative was Aaron hauling it on the bus every morning. The case had a strip of masking tape across the handle with a name in ballpoint, and the name was not his grandfather's. It was someone called R. Deslauriers, which raised questions Aaron could not answer and which nobody in his family seemed interested in answering.

He wanted to play it by the spring concert. Not perform, exactly; he had not worked out what counted. He wanted to be the kind of person who could pick up a guitar in a room and make something that wasn't noise. He had been in band since grade seven, on trumpet, and he was competent at trumpet the way he was competent at parallel parking, which was to say he could do it and it gave him no pleasure. The guitar felt different from the first afternoon he sat with it on the risers behind the percussion cabinet, though different was all he could say about it, because he could not yet make it do anything at all.

The strings were wrong. He understood this within five minutes, because he tuned the fat one to a low E on the piano in the corner and then, working upward, expected each next string to follow in some orderly way, like a scale, and instead nothing matched anything. The piano said one thing and the guitar said another, and he sat there turning the fourth peg a quarter inch at a time, listening to the gap between what he wanted and what he got, which was considerable.

"You look like a man defusing a bomb," said Marie-Soleil, who had come in for her flute lesson and stayed to watch. She dropped her backpack on a chair and leaned on the piano. "What is that thing?"

"My grandfather's. Maybe. It might be some guy named Deslauriers's." He plucked the string he'd been fighting with and let it sour in the air between them. "All the strings are tuned to something, but not to anything I know."

Laeticia arrived ten minutes later, early for the same flute lesson, and by then Aaron had written on the whiteboard in the corner the notes he'd figured out so far, in pencil so Mr. Novák wouldn't kill him. He had E on the first string, A on the second, and a question mark after that. Laeticia looked at the board, looked at the guitar, and said, "My uncle plays. Hold on, don't move."

She did not call her uncle. Instead she went to her backpack and came back with a battered spiral notebook from a summer camp two years ago, flipped through pages of friendship bracelet diagrams and swim schedules, and found a page with six letters written down the margin in green pen: E, A, D, G, B, E. "He made me memorize it the week I borrowed his guitar," she said. "From the lowest string to the highest. E, A, D, G, B, and then E again. He said everybody's uncle teaches them that eventually." She tapped the page. "It's called standard tuning."

"The lowest string is E," Aaron said slowly, "and then it goes A, D, G, B, and the highest one is E again. Like the bookends." He looked at his whiteboard, at his two lonely letters, and felt something loosen in his chest, the same feeling as when a math problem stopped being a wall and became a set of stairs. He picked up the guitar and found the fifth string, the A, already close, only a little flat, and brought it up until it rang against the piano like a matched pair.

The B string was the strange one. He had expected the pattern to continue and it broke, and Marie-Soleil said the B was where every beginner's ear gave up, and he worked at it with the piano's B for company until the two notes sat together. Then all six were in tune, E to E, and he strummed them open, all at once, and the chord that came out was enormous and slightly wrong and completely his. "That's an Em," Laeticia said. "More or less. Your G is a hair sharp." He let the sound die away and did it again.

The following weeks developed a shape. Tuesdays and Thursdays, while the flute lessons happened eight feet away, he learned three chords and then five, and his fingertips went sore and then calloused and then, somehow, his. He thought sometimes about the trumpet sitting at home in its case, and about the difference between doing something because it was expected and doing it because on Thursday afternoons the band room had that grey winter light and the three of them made a noise together that nobody had assigned. His father called it a hedonistic streak, half teasing, when Aaron skipped a Saturday of exam prep to practice; Aaron didn't argue, but he privately thought the word was wrong, that there was nothing self-indulgent about hurting your fingers on purpose for something you couldn't yet do.

Mr. Novák watched from his office doorway more than once without comment. In early March he finally came over, stood by the piano with his coffee, and asked what the plan was. Aaron said he didn't have one, exactly. He said he wanted to contextualize the guitar against what he already knew, use the trumpet reading and the band training, but he also said he didn't want to turn it into another thing he was graded on. He heard how circular it sounded as he said it. Mr. Novák considered this, sipped his coffee, and said, "The spring concert has an open slot before the senior ensemble. Two minutes. You'd have to commit." Then he went back into his office before Aaron could answer, which was, Aaron understood, itself a kind of answer.

He told Marie-Soleil and Laeticia he hadn't decided. Marie-Soleil said that was a lie told politely to oneself. She had a way of doing this, locating the exact place where his probity failed, usually in the last inch, and handing it back to him. "You've been playing for three months," she said. "You'll be nervous and you'll probably mess up the B string in front of two hundred people. That's what will happen. Decide if you want that anyway."

The concert was in May. On the last Thursday of April, the three of them stayed late, the flute lessons long since over, the janitor's vacuum going somewhere down the hall. Aaron played the piece through, a slow Em to C progression with one clumsy hammer-on he'd learned off a video, and when he finished, the room was quiet except for the vacuum. His hands were shaking a little, the way they probably would on stage, and he let them shake, and he thought about R. Deslauriers, whoever he was, and about his grandfather, and about the two Es holding everything in between. He put his thumb across the low E string and said, "From the top again. Count me in."

activity: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
knowledge_domain: to interpret a blood pressure reading and explain how diet and exercise change it
fact: White coat hypertension is when blood pressure reads high in a clinic, often from nervousness, but normal at home, so doctors may check it with home or all-day monitoring.
story:
Rachel had pinned the blood pressure cuff around Giovanni's arm for the fourth time, and for the fourth time the little screen flashed an error because he would not stop flexing.

"Stop flexing."

"I'm not flexing. That's just my arm," said Giovanni, which was a lie, because his other arm, the one without the cuff, was resting on the picnic table in a deliberate curve. Bentley sat across from them eating a granola bar with the slow patience of someone waiting for a catastrophe.

The camp had billed the afternoon as Health Science Elective, which so far meant one nurse, one classroom of borrowed equipment, and Ms. Vu, who taught biology during the school year and apparently ran this station in the summers with the cheerful ruthlessness of a general. Rachel had signed up because her mother wanted her to be a doctor, which Rachel had explained to her mother was not actually how careers worked, and her mother had replied that it was exactly how careers worked, and Rachel had signed up anyway out of spite, which she was beginning to suspect was not the best reason to learn anything.

The nurse, whose name tag read only NURSE DEB, had shown them once how to wrap the cuff, press start, and read the numbers: systolic over diastolic, the top one the pressure when the heart squeezed, the bottom one when it rested. Then she had gone to allay a crisis involving a bee sting and a crying eleven-year-old, leaving the machine and three teenagers unsupervised.

Giovanni finally held still. The cuff hissed, tightened, released. The screen offered a number that made Bentley sit up.

"That's high," Bentley said, crumbs falling from his mouth in a way that suggested deep scholarly seriousness. "Like, actually high. Like you, Giovanni, are dying."

"I am not dying. I feel incredible."

"Ms. Vu said above 130 over 80 is a thing," Bentley said, reading off the wrinkled handout as though it were scripture.

Rachel looked at the number, then at Giovanni, who was now pale in a manner that suggested he did not feel incredible at all. "Okay, but wait. Take it again."

He took it again, staring at the screen this time, gripping the table. The second number was higher. The third was higher still. Giovanni announced that his hands were cold, which they were not, and that his grandmother had died of something, though he could not name what, and that maybe he should sit down, though he was already sitting down.

"You're nervous," Rachel said.

"I'm not nervous. I'm appropriately vigilant."

"Your blood pressure is going up because you keep watching your blood pressure." She said it half as a joke, then stopped, because something snagged in her mind. Her own physical, back in June: the nurse had frowned at the reading, and the doctor had leaned back in her chair and asked, before saying anything else, what Rachel's numbers looked like at home. At the time Rachel had thought it was a strange question, like being asked your weight on the moon. But her mother had pulled out her phone with the calm of a woman who tracked everything, and the home readings were all fine, and the doctor had nodded and said the clinic number didn't count by itself.

"How do you even take it at home?" Giovanni said, staring at the machine as though it had personally insulted his grandmother.

Rachel explained what she remembered: that readings could come out high in a clinic just from nerves, but be normal at home, so doctors might not trust the office number alone; they might send you home with a monitor, or wear one for a whole day, before deciding anything. The word for it surfaced as she spoke, and she said it like she was setting it down carefully: "White coat hypertension."

"White coat," Bentley repeated, and looked down at his own camp t-shirt, and said, "I knew the outfits were a conspiracy."

Ms. Vu appeared at the table, having materialized in the crepuscular light under the awning the way she always did, without footsteps, and looked at the screen, and at Giovanni, and at Rachel. "Interesting numbers?"

"White coat hypertension," Bentley announced, with the pride of a man delivering a verdict.

"Giovanni, did you eat three helpings at lunch and run here?" Ms. Vu asked, and Giovanni admitted that he had, and she nodded as though this explained a great deal, which it might have, and told them to log it, take a reading tomorrow morning before breakfast, and compare.

Rachel wrote it down, and under her neat entry she added a smaller, less neat note to herself, which was that she did not actually know yet whether nerves explained Giovanni's numbers or only hers, or whether exercise and the camp's terrible food would pull them down or not. She drew a box around the morning reading and labeled it ASK.

"Tomorrow," she said, snapping the notebook shut, "we test you before you're awake enough to be afraid."

Giovanni flexed his arm, just once, out of principle.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: On the practical driving test in Great Britain, a candidate passes with no more than 15 driving faults and no serious or dangerous faults.
story:
Grandad's driveway had two shopping trolleys in it, which he had dragged home from the car park years ago and now used as parking cones. "Left trolley is the car in front," he said, tapping the rusty one with his stick, "right trolley is the car behind. Now get between them without murdering either." Gabrielle had been practising parallel parking for a week, and the trolleys had survived every attempt, though the right one had acquired a new dent shaped like her bumper.

Her test was on Thursday, and she was staying at her grandparents' because their street, narrow and lined with cars that never moved, was exactly like the streets examiners loved. Her friend Landen came over on Tuesday with a bag of chips and a clipboard on which he had written, in enormous letters, MOCK TEST. "Serious fault if you sneeze," he said gravely, standing at the kerb while she reversed. "You sneezed. That's a serious fault." "That's not a real thing," she said through the window. "How do you know? Have you read the rules?" He gesticulated at the clipboard, at the sky, at the general injustice of the world.

She had read the rules, actually, the night before, on her phone under the covers while Grandad watched snooker downstairs. She'd found the marking scheme and read it twice, then a third time because it seemed too generous. On the practical driving test, you could pass with up to fifteen driving faults, small things like hesitating or clipping a kerb; what you could not have was even one serious or dangerous fault. Fifteen seemed like a lot. She'd always imagined the examiner as a hawk, ready to fail her for a crooked wheel. The idea that the thing was graded, that faults came in weights, had rearranged something in her head, though she hadn't decided yet whether it made her braver or just reckless.

The trouble was the highway. On Wednesday her uncle took her out for merging practice, and the slip road near the retail park was a short ramp that emptied into fast traffic, and twice she slowed to a crawl at the bottom, waiting for a gap that the flow never offered. "You can't stop there," her uncle kept saying, not unkindly, his hands doing a rolling motion as though he could steer the oncoming lorries aside. She knew she couldn't stop there. She also knew that pulling into a gap too small was exactly the kind of thing that got a test marked with the word dangerous.

She tried to hold both ideas at once. The parking, she was learning, was about accepting small imperfection: ease back, touch the kerb lightly, correct, carry on, and the fault counted but did not sink you. The merging was the opposite discipline, about refusing to hesitate at all, because hesitation at the bottom of that ramp was itself the danger. Two different ways of thinking, and she could not fully reconcile them, only notice when to wear which one. She told Ms. Toussaint, her neighbour from across the road, who had stopped by with a plate of shortbread for Grandad and stayed to watch the trolley drills. "When I took mine, decades ago, I failed for being too cautious," Ms. Toussaint said. "Nobody warns you about that."

On Thursday morning Landen arrived with the clipboard again, which Gabrielle confiscated and hid under the spare tyre in the boot, a small subterfuge he pretended to resent. Grandad put a flask of tea in the car because, he said, examiners were human and humans ran on tea, though she suspected he just wanted to contribute something. She almost hugged the trolleys goodbye, which made Landen laugh so hard he had to lean on the gate.

The test itself went badly and then it didn't. Turning out of the test centre she stalled, which was one fault, and later she hesitated at a roundabout, another, and on the parallel park, in front of an actual parked car and an actual cone the examiner had placed, her rear wheel kissed the kerb with a small but unmistakable scrape. Her stomach dropped through the floor of the car. That sound, she was sure, was the sound of failure. The examiner made a mark on his sheet, said "carry on, please," and she drove the rest of the route in a state of grief so thorough that when he told her to pull up at the end and switch off, she was already composing the text to Landen, something short and dignified.

"Five driving faults," the examiner said. "That's a pass." Gabrielle stared at him. "But I hit the kerb." He looked at her over the sheet. "A kerb touch is a driving fault. You'd need more than fifteen of those to fail, and no serious or dangerous ones. You had neither." She signed where he pointed, her hand not quite steady, and walked back up the street to where Grandad and Landen and Ms. Toussaint had gathered at the gate like a small committee. Landen held up the clipboard, which he had somehow retrieved from the boot, and had already written, at the top, in enormous letters: FIRST TRY. "You put that there before I'd even left," she said. "Insurance," said Landen. Grandad poured the examiner's untouched tea into two cups and handed her one.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: A pencil's core is a mix of graphite and clay; more clay makes a harder pencil with lighter marks, marked H, and less clay makes a softer, darker one, marked B.
story:
Julia spread the pencils across the kitchen table in a fan, like cards she was about to read. Six of them, borrowed from Abbigail's kit, each stamped with a small letter and number. The portrait she had drawn of her grandmother the night before lay beside them, already ruined at the jaw, where her wrist had dragged a grey fog across the cheek she'd spent an hour getting right.

Abbigail leaned against the counter with her arms folded, watching Julia hold the drawing up to the window light. "Which grade did you use?"

"The one with the six and the B." Julia turned the pencil in her fingers. "It felt rich going down. Dark. I thought dark meant good."

"6B is the softest one I lent you." Abbigail pulled out the chair across from her and sat. "A pencil's core is graphite mixed with clay. More clay makes it harder and lighter, and those are the H ones. Less clay makes it softer and darker, the B ones." She plucked the 2H from the fan and scratched a thin, silvery line on the corner of a napkin. "See? Barely there. You could run your thumb over that all day."

Julia ran her thumb over the 6B patch she'd made next to it and came away with a black smudge on her skin, like she'd handled charcoal or a bruised plum. "So I've been building a portrait out of something that won't stay where I put it."

"You've been building a portrait out of midnight. It's beautiful, honestly. It just travels."

Helena arrived twenty minutes later with her bike helmet still on, because Helena believed that removing a helmet mid-visit was a commitment to staying she wasn't prepared to make. She looked at the drawing, looked at Julia's smudged hand, and said, "Fixable. Grandma's jaw, I mean. You redraw the whole side with the H pencils, light layers, and the 6B only for the pupils and the deepest folds. Dark where it matters, not everywhere." She tapped the ruined cheek with one finger, carefully, the way you'd touch a wound to see if it still hurt.

Julia didn't answer right away. She was not, by nature, someone who introspected comfortably; she preferred to think with her hands, and her hands were telling her something now, turning the 6B over, then the 2H, weighing the difference between them, which was almost nothing, grams of clay. Her whole problem was an apportionment problem. Too much soft graphite where the face needed restraint, and the drawing had paid for her greed. But she thought of Ms. He, who had told her once at the community studio that beginner drawings fail in two directions, the timid and the gluttonous, and that the gluttons usually had more talent. She wasn't sure she believed that. She wasn't sure it wasn't something kind Ms. He said to everyone.

She taped fresh paper over the smudged jaw, a patch a shade lighter than the rest, and began again with the 2H. The mark it left was so faint she had to tilt the paper toward the window to see it, a ghost of a cheekbone, impermeable to her dragging wrist. She tested it, deliberately, pressing the heel of her hand across it and rubbing. The line held. It was the first thing in three days of drawing that had stayed.

Helena made tea. Abbigail texted her mother that she'd be late. Julia worked through the layers, 2H then 4B at the fold beside the mouth, saving the 6B for last, for the pupils, exactly two small pools of it, applied with a point she sharpened with a blade because the sharpener kept breaking the soft core. When she finally set the pencil down the kitchen had gone dim and someone had turned on the stove light, and the portrait of her grandmother lay finished on the table with its pale jaw and its two dark eyes.

She still didn't know whether restraint was a virtue or just a fear that had learned better manners. Maybe both, maybe the difference didn't matter, maybe she'd find out on the next drawing. Abbigail leaned over her shoulder and said nothing for a moment, and then, "That's the best thing you've made."

Julia picked up the 2H again and wrote, in the corner where a signature would go, the letter and number, small, so she'd remember.

activity: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
knowledge_domain: to pass a driving test by practising parallel parking and merging on the highway
fact: When parallel parking, a driver usually reverses in from alongside the car in front, turning the wheel toward the curb first and then away as the car swings into the space.
story:
The bank parking lot on Sunday was empty except for a row of shopping cart corrals and, near the drive-through lane, a silver sedan belonging to the assistant manager, who had agreed to let Savannah practice between the painted lines of two imaginary spaces. Blake had brought four traffic cones borrowed from the gym shed and set them out so that the gap between the middle pair measured about a car length and a half. Savannah sat behind the wheel of her mother's hatchback with the engine running, staring into the rearview mirror as though it might offer an opinion.

"You're crooked again," Blake said from the curb, arms folded, stoic as a fence post. "Like, forty-five degrees crooked."

"I can see that." She pulled forward and reset. Her test was on Thursday, and parallel parking was the one maneuver she could not make obedient. On the highway she had learned to merge, more or less, though the on-ramp by the mall still made her hands damp: the shoulder check, the signal, the search for a gap in moving metal, all of it compressed into eight seconds of judgment. Ms. Bekele, the driving instructor, had told her that hesitation at the top of a ramp was more dangerous than imperfection, and that some drivers stigmatize learners for going slow, which was a reason to be decisive rather than a reason to be reckless. Savannah had written that in her notebook, though she suspected it was a lesson she would have to keep learning.

Back at the cones, she reversed toward the gap the way she always did, swinging wide, and ended up diagonal to the curb, the rear tire inches from a cone she could not see. She pulled out again and sat with her hands on the wheel.

"Want me to tell you when to turn?" Blake asked.

"No. If you tell me, I'll never feel it." This was the position she had arrived at after three weeks of lessons: Ms. Bekele's method, all mirrors and measurements, and her cousin's method, all feel and vibes, and neither one sufficient alone. She needed the rules to live in her hands the way they lived on the page.

On the next attempt she came in alongside the front cone, close, the way she'd been shown, and began reversing with the wheel turned toward the curb. The car's nose swung out; the rear swung in; and then, at the moment when her rear tire neared the curb, she kept turning the same way out of fear, and the whole car corkcrewed into that familiar diagonal. She stopped, breathing through her nose.

Ms. Bekele had pulled into the lot in the school's training car, apparently to collect paperwork from the branch, and stood now beside the cone watching. She didn't lecture. She raised one hand, turned it toward the curb, then rotated it slowly back the other way, and pointed at the moment in the maneuver where Savannah's rear wheel had been.

"Wait," Savannah said. "After the back end's in, I turn away from the curb?" Ms. Bekele only nodded once and went inside, coffee cup in hand.

Savannah pulled forward to reset, her mind running it backward like film. You reverse in from alongside the car in front, that much she'd had. You turn the wheel toward the curb first, and then, as the rear swings into the space, you turn the wheel away from the curb, and the body of the car straightens itself out, follows its own nose in. All this time she had been treating the parking as one continuous motion when it was two motions, a curve in and a curve out, the second one undoing the first. She felt the shape of it settle somewhere behind her sternum.

She lined up alongside the front cone, close enough to read the sticker on it. Reverse, wheel toward the curb, watching the rear corner clear the back cone in her side mirror. Then, when her rear tire was a foot from the line, she turned the wheel away, smooth, not panicked, and the hatchback swung in and flattened itself parallel to the painted line like it had been poured there. She straightened the wheel and stopped. Both cones stood. The curb sat a tidy six inches from her tire.

"Dylan owes me ten dollars," Blake said, grinning. "He said you'd hit the cone by June."

"He said that in April." Savannah was laughing before she finished the sentence, then made herself do it again, because one success could be luck and she wanted proof. Second attempt, clean. Third attempt, she overcorrected and clipped a cone with her bumper, and she felt the failure register without drowning her. She reset it and did it a fourth time, clean again, her hands already knowing the turn-back before her brain announced it.

Afterward they sat on the curb splitting a bag of grapes Blake had brought, the bank's drive-through quiet behind them. Thursday still frightened her, the examiner's clipboard, the merge onto Route 9 where the traffic never slowed. She did not know yet whether her hands would stay calm under a stranger's gaze, and she was honest enough with herself to admit that. But the two motions were hers now, curve in, curve out, and she practiced them in her head while Blake flicked grape stems into the corrals.

"One more," she said, standing, and held out her hand for the keys.
